Response to Reviewers' Comments (NCOMMS-25-86882)
We sincerely thank all the referees for their careful review of our work and for providing insightful
and constructive comments. Below, please find our detailed point-by-point responses.
Response to Reviewer #1
In their work, “Configurable plasmon polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN heterostructures”,
Y. Xie et al. report on coupled polaritons in heterostructures of carbon nanotubes (CNT) arrays and
hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). They carefully study a frequency-dependent transition of the
polaritons from hyperbolic to elliptical propagation and show indications of a whispering-gallery
plasmonic mode in a closed-loop CNT array structure. I feel their work is particularly interesting as
it explores polaritons of a relatively new material structure (CNT arrays), which here are hybridized
with hBN phonon polaritons.
Overall, I think the results are interesting, novel, and worth publishing. It appears that most of the
findings presented are well-supported by an instructive combination of experimental results,
numerical simulations, and comparison with literature. While the final section of the manuscript —
on whispering-gallery modes — presents interesting findings, it does not yet match the quality and
clarity of the rest of the manuscript and should be revised before publication.
Please find below some detailed comments.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her appreciation of our work and for the positive
evaluation. We are also very grateful for the constructive comments provided by the reviewer that
have helped us improve the manuscript. Below, we address the questions and comments raised by
the reviewer one by one.
1. The manuscript presents experimental results in a relatively broad spectral range from around
900 to >1600 cm-1, which requires a tunable or broadband light source. However, the methods
section mentions that the results have been obtained with a CO laser at a single wavelength of
2
10.6 um. Please add relevant information on the laser used for the experiments.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing out our mistake in the Methods section.
In addition to the CO laser, we also used a quantum cascade laser (QCL) with a tunable frequency
2
ranging from 900 cm-1 to 1600 cm-1 in our near-field optical measurement. We have revised the
Methods section of the manuscript and added the relevant information as follows.
“For near-field infrared nano-imaging, we employed a custom-built scattering-type scanning near-
field optical microscope (s-SNOM) that integrates a tapping-mode atomic force microscope (AFM,
Bruker Innova) with a CO laser and a Daylight Solution quantum cascade laser (QCL). The system
2
operates by focusing a mid-infrared laser (900~1650cm-1) beam onto the apex of a conductive AFM
probe, generating a highly localized enhanced optical field. This near-field interacts with the sample,
and the resulting scattered light, which encodes local optical information, is collected in the far field
using a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector (KLD-0.1-J1, Kolmar). To suppress background
scattering, the collected signal is demodulated using a lock-in amplifier (Zurich Instruments HF2LI).
This configuration allows for the simultaneous acquisition of high-resolution near-field optical
images alongside topography information during measurements.”
2. As shown in Fig. 1b and described in Supplementary Note 2, the authors simply assume the
conductivity of air for the radial direction (y-direction) of the CNT permittivity. While they state that
this is consistent with previous research on CNT arrays, the authors do not provide specific
references. The permittivity is an essential assumption that should be discussed in more detail. If
the permittivity along the y-direction was in fact slightly negative, would this mean that the
behavior qualitatively more resembled the well-studied case of graphene and the “topological
transition” with frequency may disappear?
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her insightful comments and suggestions.
For the selection of the radial dielectric constant of carbon nanotube (CNT) arrays, we adopted a
strategy that combines referencing parameters from the literature with fitting experimental
observations. Theoretically, based on the coupled Luttinger liquid theory, CNT arrays exhibit
charge-insulating properties in the radial direction [Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 676 (2001)], which aligns
with our previous studies on the material properties of CNT arrays [Science, 387, 1310 (2025)].
Based on this, we treated the radial direction as a quasi-air medium (insulating assumption). This
simplified approach has been widely adopted in the field of CNT array research [IEEE Trans.
Antennas Propag. 57 1412(2009)] [Phys. Rev. B 82 155423(2010)] [IEEE Trans. Nanotechnol. 11
964(2012)]. It has been confirmed that this parameter setting achieves excellent agreement in
reproducing the CNT hyperbolic experimental phenomena [Chinese Phys. Lett. 42, 090710 (2025)]
as well as in fitting the topological hybridization experiments in this study, thereby verifying the
robustness of the theoretical model.
Regarding the comment on the possibility that the dielectric constant in the y-direction might be
slightly negative, we conducted an in-depth analysis. In the mid-infrared range, the response of
CNT arrays in the radial (y) direction to external fields is extremely weak (the magnitude of the
dielectric constant is very small), and the dominant characteristic of the system is hyperbolic
plasmonic behavior. Simulations and corresponding iso-frequency contours (see Fig. R1 below)
show that setting the radial dielectric constant to small negative values (e.g., -2) yields results that
are nearly identical to those obtained with a value of +1. Physically, while a negative dielectric
constant supports high-momentum radial modes (manifested as short-period oscillations), these
modes are distinct from the characteristics of axial hyperbolic modes and do not significantly affect
the propagation behavior of the hyperbolic wavefront.
It is important to emphasize that only when the absolute value of the radial dielectric constant
becomes sufficiently large does the momentum of the radial mode significantly decrease, leading
to a topological phase transition from hyperbolic polaritons to elliptical polaritons (as shown in Fig.
R1f). Only under such extreme conditions would the frequency-dependent topological transition
disappear, and the system would exhibit isotropic behavior similar to graphene. Therefore, within
the current parameter range, our conclusions remain robust.
Figure R1. The influence of radial dielectric constant on the topological transition. The numerical simulated spatial
distribution of the real part of the polariton field Re(E) (top)measured above the CNT-array/hBN at frequencies of
z
1639cm-1 and corresponding iso-frequency contours (bottom) with different radial dielectric constants.
3. Regarding the whispering-gallery modes, the authors mention “the intensity of the constructive
interference peaks also oscillates with changes in frequency, revealing an inverse relationship
between peak spacing and intensity: the smaller the peak spacing, the higher the intensity”.
However, Fig. 4d shows “IR intensity” in arbitrary units. How is “intensity” defined here? I.e., how
do the authors make sure that their definition of “intensity” is consistent across different
frequencies and a frequency-dependent comparison of “intensity” is useful?
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments.
In our study, "intensity" is defined as the relative difference between the near-field signal—
specifically, the magnitude of the electric field perpendicular to the surface (|E|)—at the
z
interference-enhanced peak of CNT-array/hBN polaritons and the background level observed in
the pure hBN region. Given that hBN forms a substantial part of the substrate, providing an
overarching background, we believe this definition of intensity is appropriate. Throughout the
experiments, we maintained a consistent intensity of incident light across varying frequencies to
ensure comparability.
To enhance clarity, we have refined our statement to:
“As the two interference peaks move closer together, the interference pattern becomes more
strongly constructive.”
4. While all figures in the main manuscript use false-color maps, none of these includes a color bar.
It would be helpful to either include color bars for all false-color maps or at least provide a more
detailed description of the displayed quantities in the caption.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her kind reminder.
In our revised manuscript, we have added color bars to all false-color maps to enhance clarity.
Additionally, we have provided more detailed descriptions of the displayed quantities in the figure
captions.
5. The section on the on the whispering-gallery modes appears to include several claims that are
not well supported. Specifically, the following claims should be supported by a quantitative analysis:
a. The authors mention “near-atomic-level smooth, lossless ring-shaped interfaces”. While “lossless”
is a strong claim, no quantitative analysis of losses is provided.
b. “The high compression ratio (…) preserves quantum state coherence”. “quantum state coherence”
appears vague here and it is not clear how this statement is supported by the data.
c. The authors mention that their structures “showcase the unique benefits of Luttinger liquid
plasmons”. This should be discussed in more detail. Specifically, how are the benefits “unique”
compared to other plasmonic systems?
d. The authors mention “Compared to traditional low-dimensional plasmonic whispering-gallery
nanocavities38, its characteristic dimensions and performance have improved by nearly an order
of magnitude.” They refer to reference 38 here. As the authors claim that the performance has
increased by nearly an order of magnitude, this should be quantified by comparing suitable figures
of merit such as the quality factor. At first glance, the whispering gallery modes shown in Fig. 4 do
not appear to have a significantly higher quality compared to the ones shown in reference 38,
making a quantitative comparison important.
e. It might be helpful to support the experimental findings on the whispering-gallery modes in Fig.
4 with numerical simulations (e.g., similar to those provided in Fig. 3).
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive comments. We have addressed each
comment and suggestion point by point as outlined below.
a-c: The plasmons in CNTs have been reported to exhibit characteristics of Luttinger liquid
plasmons, demonstrating excellent properties of high spatial confinement and high quality factors,
as detailed in previous literature [Nature Photon. 9, 515-519 (2015)]. We have quantitatively
analyzed these properties using the quality factor 𝑄 =𝑅𝑒(𝑞)/𝐼𝑚(𝑞) and the compression factor
𝑁 =𝑅𝑒(𝑞)/𝑘 . Additionally, we fitted the experimental near-field profile with the following

We selected experimental data at frequencies of 1111 cm-1 and 1639 cm-1 for fitting, as shown in
Fig. R2 below. Notably, the quality factor of the CNT array plasmons reaches up to 21, while the
compression factor is 21.57. These results highlight that even structured into whispering-gallery-

To support this conclusion, we collected frequency-dependent near-field signal intensity data with

However, we acknowledge that some expressions in our manuscript are not rigorous enough and
require further refinement. For example, we have revised “lossless ring-shaped interfaces” to

Response to Reviewer #2
This manuscript presents an approach to modulate the dispersion of hyperbolic Luttinger-liquid
plasmon polaritons (HLLPPs) in carbon nanotube (CNT) arrays through coupling with phonon
polaritons (PhPs) in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). The authors demonstrate a frequency-
controlled topological transition from hyperbolic to elliptic polariton wavefronts and report the
observation of a whispering-gallery confined plasmonic mode in the coupled CNT/h-BN
heterostructure. The study addresses a topic of clear relevance to the fields of nanophotonics and
polaritonics, potentially contributing to the development of tunable hybrid polaritonic systems.
However, in my opinion, this manuscript in its current form requires major revisions to become
acceptable for publication in Nature Communications.
First, the novelty and physical interpretation need to be clarified, several claims must be
quantitatively supported, and the results should be better addressed considering previous works.
In addition, several figures and methodological descriptions require improved clarity. Addressing
these issues would significantly enhance the scientific quality and overall impact of the manuscript.
Please, find detailed comments below.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of our work and the valuable suggestions for
enhancing the manuscript. Below, we address each question and comment in detail.
1. The authors should carefully revise the manuscript to ensure consistent and precise use of
polaritonic terminology. Terms such as “plasmon polaritons”, “hybrid polaritons”, and “phonon
polaritons” appear to be used interchangeably, which can lead to conceptual ambiguity. Each
polariton type should be clearly defined and used consistently according to its physical origin and
distinctive characteristics.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions regarding the use of polaritonic
terminology.
In response, we have revised some terms throughout the manuscript. In particular, we have revised
the manuscript title from “Configurable plasmon polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN
heterostructures” to “Frequency-dependent topological polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN
heterostructures” for greater clarity.
To clarify terminology within the manuscript: “plasmon polaritons” refers to the polaritons
generated from the interaction between charges in CNT arrays and incident photons, while
“phonon polaritons” denote the interactions between phonons in hBN and photons. The term
“hybrid polaritons” describes the coupled modes resulting from plasmon and phonon polariton
interactions. Specifically, in regions outside the Reststrahlen band 2 of hBN, only plasmon
polaritons propagate in the CNT-array/hBN system. However, within the Reststrahlen band, CNT
arrays plasmon polaritons are classified as hybrid polaritons due to their coupling with phonon
polaritons in hBN.
To eliminate ambiguity, we have made these definitions consistent throughout the revised
manuscript.
2. In Supplementary Information Note 4, the authors state: “The dispersion relations are similar to
Fig. 3e, indicating reliable and accurate results.” This appears instead to refer to Figure 2e. The
authors should verify the accuracy of all internal references (figures, tables, and text sections)
throughout the manuscript.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her careful review, and for pointing out our mistake.
The typo has been corrected, as shown below.
“Here, we calculated the frequency-momentum dispersion relations of hybrid plasmons using the
finite element simulation method (COMSOL), as shown in Supplementary Figure 3. The dispersion
relations are similar to Fig.2e, indicating reliable and accurate results.”
3. In the Introduction, the authors compare plasmon polaritons in CNTs with phonon polaritons in
materials such as h-BN and α-MoO . They mention that plasmon polaritons exhibit superior
3
properties, including low loss and broad spectral range. This claim should be quantitatively
supported with comparative metrics such as propagation length, lifetime, and confinement, or
otherwise tempered. Moreover, phonon polariton systems, though spectrally limited to the
Reststrahlen bands, are typically characterized by longer lifetimes and reduced losses compared to
plasmonic systems due to their distinct scattering mechanisms. I would recommend the authors to
reference prior reports on controlled polariton propagation in phonon-polariton systems (Nano Lett.
2020, 20, 5301–5308; Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5323–5329; Nat Commun 2024, 15, 9042).
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments regarding the comparative analysis of
plasmon polaritons in CNTs and phonon polaritons in materials like h-BN and α-MoO .
backscattering in their one-dimensional structure, allowing Luttinger-liquid plasmons to achieve
high quality factors of up to 20 (Nat. Photon., 9, 515 [2015]). This quality factor is generally superior
to that of plasmons observed on other low-dimensional surfaces, such as graphene. However, we
acknowledge that CNT plasmons do not possess this advantage when compared to phonon
polaritons.
To enhance clarity and precision, we have revised the introduction with the following statement:
“ Plasmon polaritons, particularly in one-dimensional carbon nanotubes (CNTs), exhibit
exceptional properties, including deep subwavelength confinement and a broad spectral range.”
Furthermore, we have incorporated the references suggested by the reviewer (Nano Lett. 2020,
20, 5301–5308; Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5323–5329; Nat Commun 2024, 15, 9042) as citations in the
revised manuscript.
4. The authors report a topological transition of hybrid polaritons from hyperbolic to elliptic
wavefronts. Such transitions have been extensively investigated in recent literature, as they can
lead to the emergence of the so-called canalized propagation regime. It would be expected that
this system also exhibits polariton canalization at the precise topological transition frequency
(Optica 2025, 12, 343-349; Nano Lett. 2025, 25, 6, 2203–2209). The authors should discuss whether
such canalized regime is expected in the topological transition observed in the CNT array/h-BN
system. Also, the qualitative explanation of the hyperbolic-to-elliptic transition based on the sign
change of hBN’s in-plane permittivity is reasonable and consistent with established polaritonic
behavior. However, the authors show only two discrete frequency cases. A continuous evolution of
isofrequency contours across the transition region would more convincingly demonstrate the
claimed topological change.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestions regarding the topological
transition of hybrid polaritons.
The small width of our as-grown CNT arrays (only several hundred nanometers) makes it
experimentally challenging to accurately determine the excitation frequency for polariton
canalization. To address this, we have supplemented our experimental findings with analytical
calculations, as shown in Fig. R5. The results, illustrated in the figure below, show that the polariton
iso-frequency contours transition from elliptic to hyperbolic as the excitation frequency increases.
This analysis indicates that a canalization state emerges around the frequency of 1605 cm⁻¹.
Furthermore, we have incorporated the Fig. R5 as part of the revised Supplementary Information
and added the references suggested by the reviewer (Optica 2025, 12, 343-349; Nano Lett. 2025,
25, 6, 2203–2209) as citations in the revised manuscript.
Figure R5. The continuous evolution of iso-frequency contours across the transition region. The excitation
frequencies are 1585cm-1 (a), 1595cm-1 (b), 1600cm-1(c), 1605 cm-1 (d) and 1610cm-1 (e), respectively.
5. The authors describe the observed phenomena as resulting from “strong coupling” between CNT
plasmons and h-BN phonon polaritons yet no quantitative coupling parameters (e.g., mode
splitting, coupling rate, or linewidth analysis) are provided. This statement should be substantiated
with a detailed discussion of the mode splitting visible in the dispersion (Fig. 2e). For completeness,
I recommend including the individual dispersions of the CNT array and of h-BN (plots shown in the
Supplementary Information), alongside their coupled dispersion, to help the reader clearly visualize
the hybridization effect.

of the observed phenomena.

7. In Figure 1, all panels should include scale bars. If the same scale applies to multiple panels, this
should be clearly stated in the caption. Panels c and d should include a shared colorbar indicating
the plotted quantity (Re(Ez)), and panels e and f should include a grayscale colorbar for the

In the revised Figure 1, we have included scale bars in all panels. If the same scale applies to
multiple panels, this has been clearly stated in the caption. Additionally, we have added a shared

Furthermore, we have replaced the term “measured” with “simulated” in the caption to accurately
reflect the nature of the data presented. Besides, we have incorporated the references suggested

8. In Figure 2e, the authors should explain the discrepancy observed near 1400 cm-1 in the
experimental data points (high-order mode). Additionally, it would strengthen the analysis to
include error bars in the experimental estimations (blue dots) and overlay the analytical dispersion

Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s important suggestions regarding Figure 2e.
The observed discrepancy near 1400 cm-1 between the experimental data points and the calculated
dispersion relation can be attributed to measurement uncertainties. Specifically, in the frequency
region of plasmon-phonon polariton coupling, our experimental signal reflects a superposition of
the fundamental and second-order polariton modes. Due to an insufficient number of
measurement periods caused by the sample size, the extracted wavelength values may not align
perfectly with theoretical calculations.
In the revised manuscript, we have incorporated the following analysis:
“The discrepancy between the experimental data and the calculated dispersion in the Reststrahlen
band arises because our measurement captures a superposition of the fundamental and second-
order modes of the hybrid polariton.”
In response, we measured the polariton wavelength again and quantified the reading uncertainty,
with the results plotted in Fig. R7a. As can be seen, the reading error in extracting wave vectors
from the experimental data is negligible, rendering error bars virtually invisible on the plot;
therefore, they have been omitted. We attribute the observed discrepancy in the Reststrahlen
band to the experimental indistinguishability between the fundamental and higher-order modes.
Therefore, to ensure optimal visual presentation and avoid readability issues, we have chosen not
to include error bars in the experimental dispersion relation. Similar treatment has been employed
in many previously reported studies on the coupling of hBN polaritons and graphene plasmons, as
depicted in Fig. R8. [Nature Nanotech. 10, 682–686 (2015)] [Nature Mater. 14, 421–425 (2015)].

14. The coupling strength and dispersion modification in plasmon–phonon systems are known to
depend sensitively on the hBN thickness. The authors mention using a 55 nm-thick flake “to reduce

Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions regarding the dependence of
coupling strength and dispersion on hBN thickness.
Indeed, the intensity and wavelength of phonon polaritons in hBN are thickness-dependent, as
reported in previous literature [Science 343, 1125-1129 (2014)]. As indicated in Fig. R11, thicker
hBN leads to larger phonon polariton amplitude and longer polariton wavelength. In Fig. R12 below,
we simulate the coupling between polaritons in hBN flakes of varying thicknesses and CNT array
plasmons at a frequency of 1538 cm⁻¹. When the hBN flake is too thin, the resulting phonon
polaritons exhibit an extremely small amplitude and a very short wavelength. This prevents
effective coupling with plasmons in the CNT array, and the wavefront maintains its hyperbolic
character. A transition to an elliptical wavefront occurs only when the hBN thickness is sufficient.
On the other hand, since hBN serves as a substrate material, its phonon response acts as a
background signal. To prevent this phonon response from overwhelming the CNT array plasmon
signal, we cannot use excessively thick hBN. Besides, as mentioned before, the wavelength of
phonon polaritons in hBN is proportional to its thickness. Due to the size constraints of our CNT
array sample, overly thick hBN flakes produce hybrid polaritons with a wavelength that exceeds
the CNT array dimensions, thereby preventing the visualization of interference fringes. To achieve
coupling visualization between phonon polaritons and plasmons, their wavelengths need to be
comparable.
Taking all factors into consideration, we selected hBN with a thickness of several tens of
nanometers. The 55 nm thickness is not necessarily optimal; rather, it represents a suitable choice
that balances these conditions.

Response to Reviewer #3
The manuscript reports configurable plasmon–polaritons arising from the coupling between
hyperbolic plasmons and phonon polaritons in CNT array/hBN heterostructures. Infrared (IR) nano-
imaging is performed as a function of excitation laser energy, which reveals multiple branches of
coupled phonon plasmon modes. Topological transition of a hyperbolic isofrequency contour to an
elliptical one is observed using IR nano-imaging and from numerical calculations. Plasmonic
whispering-gallery modes are presented in closed-loop CNT array ring on a hBN substrate. Due to
the lack of novelty and impact of the work, and multiple significant claims with insufficient evidence
and premature data analysis, the reviewer does not recommend the publication of this manuscript
in Nature Communications.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s evaluation of our work and the valuable feedback
provided. Below, we address each question and comment raised by the reviewer one by one.
Comment 1: First and foremost, the main concern of the manuscript is the lack of novelty.
Hyperbolic polaritons have been demonstrated numerous times in other vdW materials, with
canonical examples including phonon polaritons hBN and a-MoO3 as the authors have referenced
as well as in nanopatterned hBN [Science 359, 892 (2018)]. Hyperbolic plasmons have also been
demonstrated in multiple other vdW materials, including in ZrSiSe at infrared frequencies [Sci Adv
8, add6169 (2022)] and in MoOCl2 at visible frequencies [Science 387, 786 (2025)]. The properties
claimed by the authors (deep subwavelength confinement, broad spectral range, etc) are generic
to these known (plasmonic) hyperbolic systems. Furthermore, the coupling-induced topological
transition of polaritons has been repeatedly demonstrated in other vdW materials platforms,
including in twisted a-MoO3 [Nature Mater 19, 1307 (2020); Nature 582, 209 (2020)] or in
graphene/a-MoO3 [Nature Nanotech 17, 940 (2022); Nature Commun 13, 3719 (2022)].
Therefore, the reviewer does not find that the work provides a sufficient conceptual advance to
warrant publication in Nature Communications.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thorough and systematic review of work in
this field.
We fully agree that the concept of "hyperbolic polaritons and coupling-induced topological
transitions" has been extensively studied in van der Waals materials. Therefore, the core
innovation of this work does not lie in merely reproducing this phenomenon, but rather in the
construction and validation of a novel platform with fundamentally different properties and unique
advantages for manipulation: by utilizing directly grown, ultra-clean CNT arrays as a natural
hyperbolic polariton substrate, we have achieved broadband, low-loss, and directly imageable in-
plane hyperbolic plasmons, as well as tunable topological transitions through hybridization with
hBN phonon polaritons. The distinctiveness of this platform is demonstrated in the following four
key aspects:
(1) Broadband In-Plane Hyperbolic Plasmons vs. Narrowband Phonon Hyperbolic Polaritons
The hBN, α-MoO₃, and other systems mentioned by the reviewers primarily rely on phonon
polaritons, whose hyperbolic response is constrained by the Reststrahlen band, resulting in
inherently narrow bandwidths. In contrast, our work leverages the effective medium anisotropy of
CNT arrays, where the hyperbolic behavior originates from the Luttinger-liquid plasmon properties
of CNTs. This enables high Q-factors and nearly linear dispersion over an exceptionally broad
spectral range (e.g., 6–11 μm). Our platform fundamentally differs from conventional narrowband
phonon systems in terms of bandwidth, loss levels, and mode controllability.
(2) In-Plane Wavefront Visualization and Manipulation vs. Out-of-Plane Propagation Limitations
Unlike the out-of-plane propagation or vertically quantized modes commonly observed in systems
such as ZrSiSe, our CNT array platform supports in-plane hyperbolic plasmons. This allows for direct
imaging and observation of isofrequency profiles and energy flow directions, overcoming the
geometric constraints of vertical propagation in atomically thin layers. Consequently, it enables
practical, on-demand manipulation of in-plane momentum propagation and wavefront shapes,
offering a new level of control.
(3) Ultra-Clean Direct Growth vs. Nanofabrication or Twisting Engineering
While nanopatterning techniques (e.g., etching) can induce hyperbolicity, they often introduce
edge roughness and defect scattering, which degrade performance. In contrast, our platform
employs directly grown, crystal-scale CNT arrays with atomically smooth surfaces and minimal
impurity scattering. This "ultra-clean" approach eliminates the need for complex nanofabrication
or twisting engineering, thereby directly reducing polariton transmission losses and significantly
enhancing experimental reproducibility.
(4) Universal Coupling Platform vs. Strict Frequency Matching
Regarding coupling-induced topological transitions, our work goes beyond merely replicating
existing concepts (e.g., twisted α-MoO₃) by extending them to a broadband hyperbolic plasmonic
platform. The broadband hyperbolic response of CNT arrays significantly relaxes the frequency-
matching requirements for coupled systems, functioning as a universal "coupling platform" that
allows greater design flexibility for hybridization with various polariton modes (e.g., phonons,
plasmons) without the stringent material and frequency constraints of narrowband systems.
In conclusion, the innovation of this work lies in the establishment of an ultra-clean, low-loss,
broadband, and directly imageable in-plane hyperbolic plasmon platform. This provides a scalable
and practical pathway for polariton manipulation and topological transitions without relying on
complex fabrication techniques. Our work represents a substantial advancement in the
development of polariton-based devices and tunable nanophotonics, far beyond merely
reproducing known phenomena in new materials.
Furthermore, we have incorporated the references suggested by the reviewer (Science 359, 892
(2018); Sci Adv 8, add6169 (2022); Science 387, 786 (2025); Nature Mater 19, 1307 (2020); Nature
582, 209 (2020); Nature Nanotech 17, 940 (2022); Nature Commun 13, 3719 (2022)) as citations in
the revised manuscript.
Comment 2: Another significant concern is that the manuscript repeatedly makes claims that are
not substantiated by sufficient experimental evidence or logical derivation, which compromises the
scientific integrity of the manuscript.
2-i: The claim of “configurability” based on simple frequency dependence is misleading. This is
a basic material property of CNT array/hBN device, but not an externally tunable feature that
“configurability” typically implies. The authors’ method of labelling “configurability” can
be applied to most all vdW polaritonic materials. For example, phonon polaritons in hBN exist only
within the Reststrahlen band. In this case, hBN phonon polaritons would also be “configurable”
as one can switch phonon polaritons on and off simply by tuning frequency.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her insightful comments
To prevent misunderstanding, we have revised all mentions of "configurable polaritons" in the text
to "frequency-dependent topological polaritons," and changed the title to " Frequency-dependent
topological polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN heterostructures". The polaritons reported
in this work exhibit distinct topological characteristics (hyperbolic or elliptical) depending on
frequency, which better captures the fundamental nature of this system.
We demonstrated the unique capability of our polaritons to tune their wavefront shape and
wavelength simply by adjusting the excitation frequency across a wide spectral range, an
unprecedented feature that distinguishes our system from other conventional ones. Our approach
offers an ultra-clean, efficient, and versatile solution for on-demand polariton manipulation,
completely eliminating the need for complicated twist-angle engineering in van der Waals
heterostructures or complex micro/nanofabrication of electrodes for electrostatic gating.
Therefore, this inherent advantage of our system enables direct optical control without physical
modifications or additional fabrication steps.
2-ii: The authors claim to be the “first” to demonstrate, “a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode
confined in closed-loop CNT array on hBN.” However, this claim of novelty is overstated. As the
authors' own citations (Ref. 38) confirm, whispering-gallery plasmonic modes have already been
demonstrated in other vdW materials, such as graphene. Therefore, the simple extension of this
work to a CNT array does not seem to be a significant conceptual advance, and the manuscript fails
to convey the importance of this observation in CNT arrays.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive suggestions.
We refer to being the "first" to demonstrate a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode confined in CNT
arrays. Due to the extremely small diameter of CNTs, typically around 1 nm, it is experimentally
difficult to observe whispering gallery modes within their cross-sections (such as the polariton
whispering gallery modes observed in BN nanotubes [Nat. Nanotechnol. 18, 529–534 (2023)]).
Therefore, forming CNTs into nano-rings is essential to achieve this phenomenon. We are the first
to assemble CNTs into close-loop nano-rings, and have observed a plasmonic whispering gallery
mode with a very high quality-factor (as described in the following Fig. R18) and excellent
coherence.
To prevent any misunderstanding, we have removed the word "first" from the revised manuscript.
2-iii: In addition, the authors’ claim of a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode itself is not convincing.
Plasmonic whispering gallery modes are those that travel around a circumference of the cavity.
Based on the main dataset shown in Fig. 4c, the reviewer does not see any clear signatures of
plasmonic wave travel around the circular, donut shaped structure, forming a whispering-gallery
mode. IR nano-imaging shown in Fig. 4c seems rather a result of tip-launched (or cavity edge
launched) plasmons interacting with the entire cavity structure, forming a cavity-like nano-IR
response, but not necessarily a whispering-gallery mode specific to the chiral motion of polaritons
around the loop. More rigorous analysis needs to be performed to support their claim of
whispering-gallery modes.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable feedback regarding the interpretation of the
observed phenomena as whispering-gallery plasmonic modes.
The polaritons we observe are excited by an AFM tip and propagate along the axial direction of
carbon nanotubes, completing a full loop before being detected again by the tip. Since our ring-
shaped CNT array is highly centrosymmetric and perfectly circular, when the tip is positioned above
a path at the same radius, the excitation of polaritons is identical, and the detected signals are also
identical. This is manifested as completely identical infrared signals along the same radial path in
the final near-field imaging.
However, paths at different radii display varying brightness—either brighter or darker—
corresponding to the constructive or destructive interference of the polaritons. Notably, this
brightness contrast changes with the excitation frequency, which we attribute to the presence of
the whispering-gallery mode of polaritons.
To further support our claim that these are indeed whispering-gallery modes propagating along
the axial direction of the CNT array—as opposed to radial propagation modes— we have selected
a larger closed-loop CNT array ring for analysis. The results, presented in Fig. R16, illustrate that
the path length for polaritons to complete one loop (i.e., the circumference of the circle) is
significantly longer, far exceeding the propagation distance of the polaritons. As a result, no
constructive or destructive interferences are observed in this configuration.

concerning because they are presented without any supporting evidence. At the very least, the
authors should provide a quantitative comparison of the polariton quality factors in their straight
and circular structures.

As previously noted, although hBN supports out-of-plane hyperbolic phonon polaritons, these do
not directly govern the coupling and topological transitions of in-plane hyperbolic plasmons in the
CNT array/hBN system. Specifically, within Reststrahlen band 2, hBN exhibits in-plane isotropy and
out-of-plane hyperbolic anisotropy. Due to finite thickness effects, the out-of-plane hyperbolic
dispersion of hBN is quantized, which in turn modulates the size of the in-plane circular
isofrequency contours. Consequently, it is not the out-of-plane hyperbolic dispersion itself that
directly participates in the hybrid coupling within the CNT array/hBN heterostructure; rather, it is
the in-plane isofrequency contours—tuned by the hBN thickness—that determine the
momentum-matching conditions with CNT plasmons.

and wavelength of hBN phonon polariton depends on thickness [Science 343, 1125-1129 (2014)].

wavelength. Numerical simulations for the coupling between polaritons in hBN of varying flake

amplitude and a very short wavelength of hBN phonon polaritons. A transition to an elliptical
wavefront occurs only when the hBN thickness is sufficient.

a substrate, its phonon response serves as a background signal. Overly thick hBN will mask the
plasmon signal from the CNT array. Additionally, as previously noted, the wavelength of phonon
polaritons in hBN scales with its thickness. Given the finite size of our CNT array sample, overly
thick hBN flakes generate hybrid polaritons with wavelengths that exceed the spatial dimensions
of the array, precluding the observation of interference fringes. To enable clear visualization of the
coupling between phonon polaritons and plasmons, their wavelengths must be comparable.

of several tens of nanometers—suitable for our purpose, though not necessarily the optimal
choice.

open and closed-loop shape of the IFC, is this correct? If so, this could be clarified.

the iso-frequency contours shape, rather than topological protection. This concept have been
extensively studied and reported in the field of nanophotonics, as documented in the following
references: [Nature 582, 209–213 (2020)][Nat. Nanotechnol. 17, 940–946 (2022)][Nat. Mater.

following explanation:
“Here, with a homemade scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (s-SNOM), we
experimentally demonstrate nanoscale frequency-dependent topological polaritons—specifically,
the topological transition of polariton iso-frequency contours between open and closed-loop
shapes, in CNT-array/hBN heterostructures.’’
2. The authors now mention “as the two interference peaks move closer together, the interference
pattern becomes more strongly constructive”. The authors could further clarify how
“constructiveness” can be quantified/seen from Fig. 4c.

To clarify the concept of "constructiveness", we extracted the near-field intensity profile (reflecting
the magnitude of the E component) from Fig. 4c and plotted it in Fig. 4e. The relationship between
z
the peak-to-peak distance and the peak height in the profile curve of Fig. 4e is shown in the Fig.
R1. It can be observed that a smaller peak-to-peak distance corresponds to a higher resonance
peak, indicating a more strongly constructive interference pattern.
Figure R1. The relationship between the peak-to-peak distance and the peak height of the constructive
interference peak. These data were extracted from the Fig.4e of the manuscript.
3. Regarding the whispering-gallery modes, the added comparison with the numerical simulations
is helpful. However, some comments are still not sufficiently clear. In their response and revised
supplementary information, the authors mention “The results (see Supplementary Fig. 9b), which
exhibit a strong fit to a standard resonance peak curve, confirm the presence of a whispering-
gallery mode.” It is not clear to me why “a strong fit to a standard resonance peak curve” should
indicate whispering-gallery mode polaritons. Rather a “standard” resonance peak curve should
have various possible explanations, with whispering-gallery mode polaritons being only one of
many. As such, the authors should clarify which parts of the results confirm the presence of a
whispering-gallery mode.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive comments.
A standard resonance peak curve indicates the presence of polariton interference resonance within
the array, which we attribute to the whispering‑gallery mode of polaritons. To better explain the
whispering gallery mode, we performed further numerical simulations. The results are shown in
the Fig. R2.
In these simulations, we maintained the radial width of the CNT array consistent with that of the
experimental sample while appropriately increasing the axial length to observe more periods. To
intuitively visualize the phase information of the polaritons, we placed an electric dipole above the
array to excite the polaritons and extracted the Re(E) component from above the array.
z
The simulation results clearly demonstrate the characteristics of whispering gallery modes of the
polaritons. As the incident frequency increases, the polariton wavelength decreases, and the
number of interference nodes in the standing wave increases.
Moreover, these simulation results align with our experimentally observed tip-excite-and-tip-
probe conditions, confirming that constructive interference manifests in circular patterns with
varying perimeters, consistent with the behavior expected from whispering-gallery modes.

no constructive or destructive interferences are observed in this configuration.”

excitation frequency, displaying nearly no interference. a, AFM topography image of a closed-loop CNT array ring

manuscript still indicates a broader “performance” improvement by “nearly an order of magnitude”.

Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her significant suggestions.
The reviewer is correct that the improvement solely refers to the mode volume. To clarify the
comparison, we have revised the statement as follows,
“Compared to traditional low-dimensional polaritonic whispering-gallery nanocavities, its
characteristic dimensions have improved by nearly an order of magnitude. Its mode volume is as

recommendation for the publication of our manuscript.
Response to Reviewer #3:
The authors have made a significant improvement of the manuscript and clearly addressed most
of my previous comments. Before the acceptance of the manuscript, I just a have a few minor points
that need to be clarified and would further strengthen the manuscript.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her appreciation of our work and for the
positive evaluation.
1) Q-factor of 60 derived from the frequency dependent measurements of a cavity is exceptionally
high. Can the authors explain why such a high Q-factor is possible? This three-fold enhancement
compared to Q-factors of 20 in straight devices derived by the authors is counterintuitive. Either
the specific method of extracting Q-factor of 60 is inaccurate or there is an unknown procedure
that enhances the Q-factor in a closed-loop CNT array versus a straight CNT array. This point should
be clarified.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her careful review and insightful comments.
The Q-factor of 20 was obtained by fitting the data from straight CNT array devices under
excitations at 1111 cm⁻¹ and 1639 cm⁻¹. Both frequencies lie outside the Reststrahlen band of hBN,
meaning no coupling with hBN phonon polaritons. This value reflects the intrinsic Q-factor of the
CNT array plasmons.
In contrast, the Q-factor of 60 was derived from the resonant peak's center frequency near 1600
cm⁻¹, which falls within the Reststrahlen band of hBN. Therefore, this value represents the Q-factor
of the hybrid polaritons resulting from the coupling between the CNT array plasmons and hBN
phonon polaritons. The intrinsically high Q-factor of hBN phonon polaritons (which experience zero
electronic loss) contributes to the enhanced Q-factor observed in the hybrid system.
Furthermore, polaritons propagating within a nanocavity can exhibit further enhanced Q-factors.
Previous literature has reported the Q-factor of hBN phonon polaritons in optical microcavities
reaching values as high as 100~400 [Nat. Commun. 8, 15624 (2017)] [Nat. Mater. 23, 499–505
(2024)].
These factors collectively explain the observed enhancement of the Q-factor from 20 in straight
devices to 60 in closed-loop CNT arrays.
2) Whispering gallery mode, WGM, scenario is still not fully clear based on the data itself. Could the
authors potentially show a more direct visualization of the WGM, e.g., by placing a gold launcher
at one location of the (larger) closed-loop array to visualize the propagating/circulating WGM?
Another simple point to check is whether the WGM wavelength between 1563-1593 cm-1 in a
resonance condition. Can the authors compare the round-trip distance around the cavity with
respect to the mode wavelength, and confirm if the resonance condition matches the experimental
observations?
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments and helpful suggestions.
Unfortunately, fabricating a gold launcher directly on the CNT array would introduce polymeric
residues and contaminants that are nearly impossible to completely eliminate. Given the small size
of the sample, these contaminations would significantly increase the loss of polaritons and severely
compromise the acquisition of near-field optical signals. As a result, this approach is experimentally
unfeasible.
To address the reviewer’s question, we conducted additional numerical simulations, the results of
which are presented in Figure R4. To align with the experimental conditions, we set the radial width
of the CNT array equal to that of the experimental sample while intentionally extending the axial
length to observe more oscillation periods. For clearer visualization of the polariton phase
distribution, we positioned an electric dipole (indicated by the blue dot in Figure R4a) above the
array to excite the polaritons and extracted the Re(Ez) component directly above the array.
The simulations clearly reveal the characteristics of whispering-gallery modes of the polaritons; as
the incident frequency increases, the polariton wavelength decreases, resulting in more
interference nodes within the standing wave pattern.
Figure R4. The evolution of whispering-gallery mode of polaritons in CNT-array/hBN at different frequencies. The
excitation frequencies are 1563cm-1 (a), 1575cm-1 (b), 1595cm-1(c), 1600 cm-1 (d) and 1634cm-1 (e), respectively.
The blue dot in (a) represents the electric dipole for exciting the polaritons. The dashing black circles represents
the boundary of the CNT array loop.
Furthermore, the direct fabrication of gold launchers without residual contamination on CNT arrays
poses significant challenges, preventing the extraction of polariton phase information from
experiments or the precise determination of their wavelengths for comparison. According to the
polariton dispersion relation, the theoretical wavelength range is between 600 and 1000 nm,
roughly matching the circumference of a single ring in the CNT array.
Additionally, previous studies have shown that when the cavity size is reduced to approximately
~𝜆 , polariton modes are dominated by standing waves confined along the cavity circumference
𝑝
[Nat. Mater. 22, 838–843 (2023)]. However, the quantitative conditions for low-order standing
wave resonances remain challenging to analyze at this cavity size [Nat. Commun. 8, 15624 (2017)].
In conclusion, it remains uncertain whether the resonance conditions are strictly satisfied.
Therefore, we propose that CNT arrays support standing wave interference induced by whispering-
gallery modes, which may manifest as either constructive or destructive interference. However,
the specific resonance mode cannot yet be definitively identified from the available experimental
data.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their careful evaluation of our work and for their insightful and

Response to Reviewer #1:
The authors addressed all my comments, and the manuscript appears publishable without further
revision.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her appreciation of our work and
recommendation for the publication of our manuscript.
Response to Reviewer #3:
While the reviewer agrees that hybridization with hBN phonon polaritons can enhance Q-factor,
the authors need to show quantitative evidence of Q-factor enhancement up to 60. Since high
quality factor WGM is one of the central claims of the paper, emphasized both in abstract and main
text, these points need to be clarified and the derivation and analysis of Q-factor needs to be more
rigorously presented.
Besides, based on the additional simulations provided by the authors (Figure R2), the peak in their
spectral evolution of near-field signal in a fixed on position within WGM cavity appears to be related
to a geometric effect. Near field amplitude under the tip results from tip-launched polaritons under
the tip interfering with those making a round-trip across the circumference of cavity. Changing
frequency changes WGM wavelength, which shifts the phase of round-trip polaritons with respect
to those launched under the tip. When frequency is continuously swept, this continuous increase in
the relative phase shift will lead to destructive and to constructive and back to destructive
interference, which looks like a peak in spectra. Q-factor derived from the FWHM of the standard
fitting to this peak then does not (accurately) reflect the loss of WGM. Can the authors clarify this
point?
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments and helpful suggestions.
First, we wish to clarify the core novelty of our manuscript lies in the discovery of frequency-
dependent topological polaritons arising from the coupling between hyperbolic plasmons and
phonon polaritons in CNT-array/hBN heterostructures. In particular, we achieved a controllable
topological transition of the polariton wavefront from hyperbolic to elliptical. The whispering-
gallery mode (WGM) presented here serves as a natural extension and an in-depth investigation of
this hybrid polariton mode, providing quantitative evidence of its low-loss characteristics and
enhanced coherence
We agree with the reviewer’s physical interpretation that the resonance peak of the WGM
observed in our fixed-position near-field measurement may arise from the interference between
the tip-launched field and the field that has completed one round trip along the cavity
circumference. Consequently, the linewidth of such a peak should not be directly and exclusively
interpreted as the intrinsic material loss.
In response, we wish to offer the following clarification:
1. The "Geometric Effect" is the Essence of Cavity Resonance:
The "geometric effect", i.e., the round-trip phase-matching condition requiring an integer multiple
of 2𝜋 along the circumference, is precisely the fundamental physical mechanism underlying all
optical microcavities, including whispering-gallery mode cavities and Fabry-Perot resonators. In
this context, the resonance linewidth is governed by two factors: (a) the intrinsic propagation loss
of the polaritons (including attenuation, radiation, and boundary scattering) and (b) the phase
accumulation in the closed-loop geometry.
2. The Linewidth is a Valid Proxy for Loss:
In such interference-based resonant cavities, the contrast and sharpness of the resonance peak are
inherently limited by the intrinsic propagation loss of the polaritons within the cavity.
If the propagation loss is high (short propagation length), the signal returning after one or multiple
round trips is too weak to interfere significantly, resulting in a broad, low-contrast spectral fringe
(corresponding to a low Q-factor). Conversely, if the propagation loss is extremely low, as achieved
here through hybridization with low-loss hBN phonon polaritons, the polaritons survive for
multiple round trips, enabling sharp constructive interference and a narrow spectral linewidth
(corresponding to a high Q-factor).
Therefore, fitting the resonance peak to extract ∆𝜔 and calculating 𝑄 =
𝜔𝑐
is a standard and
∆𝜔
rigorous approach in nanophotonics and cavity physics to assess the effective Q-factor of a
resonant mode. The extracted value of Q≈60 from our fitting indeed reflects the intrinsically low-
loss nature and enhanced coherence of the closed-loop CNT/hBN hybrid polariton WGM resonance.
Revision in Supplementary Information:
To prevent over-interpretation, we have added the relevant section to explicitly define this value
as the "effective Q-factor":
“We now explicitly describe the extracted value as the effective Q-factor under our specific near-
field excitation and detection conditions, rather than the intrinsic material Q. We clarify that the
linewidth is determined by both the round-trip attenuation and the phase-matching. Therefore, the
Q-factor extracted from the FWHM provides an upper-bound estimate of the lifetime of the
circulating hybrid polariton mode.”

the peak-to-peak distance and the peak height in the profile curve of Fig. 4e is shown in the Fig.
R1. It can be observed that a smaller peak-to-peak distance corresponds to a higher resonance
peak, indicating a more strongly constructive interference pattern.
Figure R1. The relationship between the peak-to-peak distance and the peak height of the constructive
interference peak. These data were extracted from the Fig.4e of the manuscript.
3. Regarding the whispering-gallery modes, the added comparison with the numerical simulations
is helpful. However, some comments are still not sufficiently clear. In their response and revised
supplementary information, the authors mention “The results (see Supplementary Fig. 9b), which
exhibit a strong fit to a standard resonance peak curve, confirm the presence of a whispering-

Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive comments.
A standard resonance peak curve indicates the presence of polariton interference resonance within
the array, which we attribute to the whispering‑gallery mode of polaritons. To better explain the
whispering gallery mode, we performed further numerical simulations. The results are shown in
the Fig. R2.
In these simulations, we maintained the radial width of the CNT array consistent with that of the
experimental sample while appropriately increasing the axial length to observe more periods. To
intuitively visualize the phase information of the polaritons, we placed an electric dipole above the
array to excite the polaritons and extracted the Re(E) component from above the array.
z
The simulation results clearly demonstrate the characteristics of whispering gallery modes of the
polaritons. As the incident frequency increases, the polariton wavelength decreases, and the
number of interference nodes in the standing wave increases.
Moreover, these simulation results align with our experimentally observed tip-excite-and-tip-
probe conditions, confirming that constructive interference manifests in circular patterns with
varying perimeters, consistent with the behavior expected from whispering-gallery modes.
Figure R2. The evolution of whispering-gallery mode of polaritons in CNT-array/hBN at different frequencies. The
excitation frequencies are 1563cm-1 (a), 1575cm-1 (b), 1595cm-1(c), 1600 cm-1 (d) and 1634cm-1 (e), respectively.

Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her significant suggestions.
The reviewer is correct that the improvement solely refers to the mode volume. To clarify the
comparison, we have revised the statement as follows,
“Compared to traditional low-dimensional polaritonic whispering-gallery nanocavities, its
characteristic dimensions have improved by nearly an order of magnitude. Its mode volume is as

Response to Reviewer #2:
The authors have adequately addressed my comments. I recommend publication in its present form.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her appreciation of our work and
recommendation for the publication of our manuscript.
Response to Reviewer #3:
The authors have made a significant improvement of the manuscript and clearly addressed most
of my previous comments. Before the acceptance of the manuscript, I just a have a few minor points
that need to be clarified and would further strengthen the manuscript.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her appreciation of our work and for the
positive evaluation.
1) Q-factor of 60 derived from the frequency dependent measurements of a cavity is exceptionally
high. Can the authors explain why such a high Q-factor is possible? This three-fold enhancement
compared to Q-factors of 20 in straight devices derived by the authors is counterintuitive. Either
the specific method of extracting Q-factor of 60 is inaccurate or there is an unknown procedure
that enhances the Q-factor in a closed-loop CNT array versus a straight CNT array. This point should
be clarified.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her careful review and insightful comments.
The Q-factor of 20 was obtained by fitting the data from straight CNT array devices under
excitations at 1111 cm⁻¹ and 1639 cm⁻¹. Both frequencies lie outside the Reststrahlen band of hBN,
meaning no coupling with hBN phonon polaritons. This value reflects the intrinsic Q-factor of the
CNT array plasmons.
In contrast, the Q-factor of 60 was derived from the resonant peak's center frequency near 1600
cm⁻¹, which falls within the Reststrahlen band of hBN. Therefore, this value represents the Q-factor
of the hybrid polaritons resulting from the coupling between the CNT array plasmons and hBN
phonon polaritons. The intrinsically high Q-factor of hBN phonon polaritons (which experience zero
electronic loss) contributes to the enhanced Q-factor observed in the hybrid system.
Furthermore, polaritons propagating within a nanocavity can exhibit further enhanced Q-factors.
Previous literature has reported the Q-factor of hBN phonon polaritons in optical microcavities
reaching values as high as 100~400 [Nat. Commun. 8, 15624 (2017)] [Nat. Mater. 23, 499–505
(2024)].
These factors collectively explain the observed enhancement of the Q-factor from 20 in straight
devices to 60 in closed-loop CNT arrays.
2) Whispering gallery mode, WGM, scenario is still not fully clear based on the data itself. Could the
authors potentially show a more direct visualization of the WGM, e.g., by placing a gold launcher
at one location of the (larger) closed-loop array to visualize the propagating/circulating WGM?
Another simple point to check is whether the WGM wavelength between 1563-1593 cm-1 in a
resonance condition. Can the authors compare the round-trip distance around the cavity with
respect to the mode wavelength, and confirm if the resonance condition matches the experimental
observations?
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments and helpful suggestions.
Unfortunately, fabricating a gold launcher directly on the CNT array would introduce polymeric
residues and contaminants that are nearly impossible to completely eliminate. Given the small size
of the sample, these contaminations would significantly increase the loss of polaritons and severely
compromise the acquisition of near-field optical signals. As a result, this approach is experimentally
unfeasible.
To address the reviewer’s question, we conducted additional numerical simulations, the results of
which are presented in Figure R4. To align with the experimental conditions, we set the radial width
of the CNT array equal to that of the experimental sample while intentionally extending the axial
length to observe more oscillation periods. For clearer visualization of the polariton phase
distribution, we positioned an electric dipole (indicated by the blue dot in Figure R4a) above the
array to excite the polaritons and extracted the Re(Ez) component directly above the array.
The simulations clearly reveal the characteristics of whispering-gallery modes of the polaritons; as
the incident frequency increases, the polariton wavelength decreases, resulting in more
interference nodes within the standing wave pattern.
Figure R4. The evolution of whispering-gallery mode of polaritons in CNT-array/hBN at different frequencies. The
excitation frequencies are 1563cm-1 (a), 1575cm-1 (b), 1595cm-1(c), 1600 cm-1 (d) and 1634cm-1 (e), respectively.
The blue dot in (a) represents the electric dipole for exciting the polaritons. The dashing black circles represents
the boundary of the CNT array loop.
Furthermore, the direct fabrication of gold launchers without residual contamination on CNT arrays
poses significant challenges, preventing the extraction of polariton phase information from
experiments or the precise determination of their wavelengths for comparison. According to the
polariton dispersion relation, the theoretical wavelength range is between 600 and 1000 nm,
roughly matching the circumference of a single ring in the CNT array.
Additionally, previous studies have shown that when the cavity size is reduced to approximately
~𝜆 , polariton modes are dominated by standing waves confined along the cavity circumference
𝑝
[Nat. Mater. 22, 838–843 (2023)]. However, the quantitative conditions for low-order standing
wave resonances remain challenging to analyze at this cavity size [Nat. Commun. 8, 15624 (2017)].
In conclusion, it remains uncertain whether the resonance conditions are strictly satisfied.
Therefore, we propose that CNT arrays support standing wave interference induced by whispering-
gallery modes, which may manifest as either constructive or destructive interference. However,
the specific resonance mode cannot yet be definitively identified from the available experimental
data.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
While the reviewer agrees that hybridization with hBN phonon polaritons can enhance Q-factor, the authors need to show quantitative evidence of Q-factor enhancement up to 60. Since high quality factor WGM is one of the central claims of the paper, emphasized both in abstract and main text, these points need to be clarified and the derivation and analysis of Q-factor needs to be more rigorously presented.
Besides, based on the additional simulations provided by the authors (Figure R2), the peak in their spectral evolution of near-field signal in a fixed on position within WGM cavity appears to be related to a geometric effect. Near field amplitude under the tip results from tip-launched polaritons under the tip interfering with those making a round-trip across the circumference of cavity. Changing frequency changes WGM wavelength, which shifts the phase of round-trip polaritons with respect to those launched under the tip. When frequency is continuously swept, this continuous increase in the relative phase shift will lead to destructive and to constructive and back to destructive interference, which looks like a peak in spectra. Q-factor derived from the FWHM of the standard fitting to this peak then does not (accurately) reflect the loss of WGM. Can the authors clarify this point?

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their careful evaluation of our work and for their insightful and
constructive feedback. Below are our detailed point-by-point responses.

Besides, based on the additional simulations provided by the authors (Figure R2), the peak in their

to a geometric effect. Near field amplitude under the tip results from tip-launched polaritons under
the tip interfering with those making a round-trip across the circumference of cavity. Changing

fitting to this peak then does not (accurately) reflect the loss of WGM. Can the authors clarify this

Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments and helpful suggestions.
First, we wish to clarify the core novelty of our manuscript lies in the discovery of frequency-
dependent topological polaritons arising from the coupling between hyperbolic plasmons and
phonon polaritons in CNT-array/hBN heterostructures. In particular, we achieved a controllable
topological transition of the polariton wavefront from hyperbolic to elliptical. The whispering-
gallery mode (WGM) presented here serves as a natural extension and an in-depth investigation of
this hybrid polariton mode, providing quantitative evidence of its low-loss characteristics and
enhanced coherence
We agree with the reviewer’s physical interpretation that the resonance peak of the WGM
observed in our fixed-position near-field measurement may arise from the interference between
the tip-launched field and the field that has completed one round trip along the cavity
circumference. Consequently, the linewidth of such a peak should not be directly and exclusively
interpreted as the intrinsic material loss.
In response, we wish to offer the following clarification:
1. The "Geometric Effect" is the Essence of Cavity Resonance:
The "geometric effect", i.e., the round-trip phase-matching condition requiring an integer multiple
of 2𝜋 along the circumference, is precisely the fundamental physical mechanism underlying all
optical microcavities, including whispering-gallery mode cavities and Fabry-Perot resonators. In
this context, the resonance linewidth is governed by two factors: (a) the intrinsic propagation loss
of the polaritons (including attenuation, radiation, and boundary scattering) and (b) the phase
accumulation in the closed-loop geometry.
2. The Linewidth is a Valid Proxy for Loss:
In such interference-based resonant cavities, the contrast and sharpness of the resonance peak are
inherently limited by the intrinsic propagation loss of the polaritons within the cavity.
If the propagation loss is high (short propagation length), the signal returning after one or multiple
round trips is too weak to interfere significantly, resulting in a broad, low-contrast spectral fringe
(corresponding to a low Q-factor). Conversely, if the propagation loss is extremely low, as achieved
here through hybridization with low-loss hBN phonon polaritons, the polaritons survive for
multiple round trips, enabling sharp constructive interference and a narrow spectral linewidth
(corresponding to a high Q-factor).
Therefore, fitting the resonance peak to extract ∆𝜔 and calculating 𝑄 =
𝜔𝑐
is a standard and
∆𝜔
rigorous approach in nanophotonics and cavity physics to assess the effective Q-factor of a
resonant mode. The extracted value of Q≈60 from our fitting indeed reflects the intrinsically low-
loss nature and enhanced coherence of the closed-loop CNT/hBN hybrid polariton WGM resonance.
Revision in Supplementary Information:
To prevent over-interpretation, we have added the relevant section to explicitly define this value
as the "effective Q-factor":
“We now explicitly describe the extracted value as the effective Q-factor under our specific near-
field excitation and detection conditions, rather than the intrinsic material Q. We clarify that the
linewidth is determined by both the round-trip attenuation and the phase-matching. Therefore, the
Q-factor extracted from the FWHM provides an upper-bound estimate of the lifetime of the
circulating hybrid polariton mode.”
