review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Plasmons in carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have attracted significant attention due to their strong spatial confinement and high-quality factors. However, constrained by CNTs’ intrinsic electronic characteristics, modulation of their plasmon dispersion relations remains a significant challenge. Here, we report frequency-dependent topological polaritons arising from the coupling between hyperbolic plasmons and phonon polaritons in CNT-array/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) heterostructures. In particular, we achieved a controllable topological transition of the polariton wavefront from hyperbolic to elliptical. Moreover, we demonstrated a whispering-gallery polaritonic mode confined in closed-loop CNT array on hBN. Our findings provide fundamental insights into optical topological transitions in low-dimensional heterostructures, and a promising route to manipulate light propagation and energy transfer at the nanoscale.

---

## Introduction

Polaritons, hybrid quasiparticles resulting from the coupling between collective oscillations of particles in materials and electromagnetic waves, have demonstrated remarkable potential of nanophotonic engineering for manipulating light-matter interactions1, 2, 3. Notably, in hyperbolic media, such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and α-phase molybdenum trioxide (α-MoO3)10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, phonon polaritons exhibit pronounced directional anisotropy, with their isofrequency curves and propagation wavefronts forming distinct hyperbola-like shapes. Furthermore, control over the propagation direction of these hyperbolic polaritons through layer stacking and twist angles has been widely reported19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26. Yet, the limited spectral range of these phonon polaritons has significantly hindered their practical applications. Plasmon polaritons27, 28, particularly in one-dimensional carbon nanotubes (CNTs)29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, present exceptional properties, including deep subwavelength confinement and broad spectral range. Recently, closely packed homochiral CNT arrays have been successfully fabricated36, and signature of hyperbolic Luttinger-liquid plasmons have been reported in this distinct material structure37. However, despite their extraordinary properties, control of the dispersion relation or isofrequency contour of the plasmons in CNT arrays has so far remained unexplored yet.

Here, with a homemade scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (s-SNOM), we experimentally demonstrate nanoscale frequency-dependent topological polaritons—specifically, the topological transition of polariton iso-frequency contours between open and closed-loop shapes, in CNT-array/hBN heterostructures. Our results achieved control over the polariton dispersion, topology, and propagation by simply tuning the excitation frequency. The control is achieved through strong coupling between anisotropic Luttinger-liquid plasmons in close-packed identical CNT arrays and in-plane isotropic phonon polaritons in hBN when the excitation frequency lies within the Reststrahlen band of hBN substrate, leading to a topological transition of plasmon isofrequency contour that evolves from hyperbolic to elliptical. Furthermore, using closed-loop CNT arrays as circular nanoscale resonators and leveraging the high-quality factor of the coupled mode, we demonstrated polaritonic whispering-gallery modes in these closed-loop CNT arrays. Our study offers an alternative avenue to control nanoscale light through strong light-matter interaction, and a paradigm for applications in compact nanophotonic devices.

---

## Results

Material structure, measurement scheme, and working principle

Our material structure composed of a close-packed array of identical CNTs on hBN substrate, a schematic of which is depicted in Fig. 1a. To quantitively analyze polariton modes within the CNT-array/hBN heterostructure, we carried out numerical simulations of the eigen electromagnetic modes in the structure using a finite element method (COMSOL Multiphysics). The structure is modeled as a dielectric medium composed of an in-plane strongly anisotropic layer38, 39, 40—representing the CNT array, and an in-plane isotropic layer—representing the hBN flake. The specific dielectric function used in our simulation can be found in Fig. 1b (see more details in Supplementary Note 2). An electrical dipole is placed at the center of the plane and serves as the excitation source. Numerically simulated field distributions of hybrid polariton modes at two representative excitation frequencies (943 cm-1 and 1538 cm-1) are shown in Figs.1c and 1d, respectively. At excitation frequency of 943 cm-1, the wavefront of the polariton mode exhibits hyperbolic. The hyperbolic plasmon originates from the strongly anisotropic conductivities of the layer of CNT array between the axial direction (x-direction) and the radial direction (y-direction). At excitation of 1538 cm-1, the wavefront becomes elliptical. The topological change of the wavefront is a result of the dramatic change in the dielectric function of the hBN layer.

It has been widely known that the two Reststrahlen bands (type I and II) of hBN support the propagation of phonon polaritons4, 7, 8. The type I band with out-of-plane dielectric function 𝜀 < 0 and in-plane dielectric function 𝜀 > 0 , extends over the frequency range 𝜔 = 760~825 cm−1 , and the type II band with 𝜀 > 0 and 𝜀 < 0 , spans the range 𝜔 = 1360~1614 cm−1. In this study, we focus exclusively on the analysis of polaritons at frequency range around the type II band. When the frequency is outside the type II Reststrahlen band, hBN exhibits positive in-plane permittivity (depicted in Fig. 1b), and no phonon polaritons are supported. As a consequence, the wavefront of plasmons in the CNT array is hyperbolic, representing the intrinsic plasmon mode of the CNT array. Once the frequency (e.g., 1538cm-1) falls into the type II Reststrahlen band, a topological transition occurs and the wavefront transforms into an elliptical shape, owing to the negative isotropic in-plane permittivity of hBN. Noted that the frequency at which this topological transition occurs is conditioned to the appearance of well-defined phonon polaritons in hBN. The strong coupling between hyperbolic plasmons in CNT array and isotropic in-plane phonon polaritons in hBN results in the elliptical-shaped wavefront. Figs.1e and 1f illustrate the corresponding Fourier transform of Figs.1c and 1d, where the yellow lines represent the fitted hyperbolic and elliptical isofrequency contour, respectively.

To experimentally demonstrate the inter-layer polariton coupling and the topological transition, we grew close-packed CNT arrays on hBN substrate using chemical vapor deposition (CVD)36, 41, 42; further details are provided in the Method section. Notably, the CNTs within each array exhibit uniform chirality and a close-packed arrangement, allowing the CNT array to be effectively described and modeled as an effective anisotropic medium36 (see more details in Supplementary Note 1). Infrared nano-imaging of the polariton response in the CNT array is achieved through a home-made s-SNOM, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. A gold-coated atomic force microscope (AFM) tip, illuminated by an infrared beam, serves as an exciter to launch polaritons in the CNT arrays. The excited polaritons propagate along the surface and reflect at the ends of the CNT array. The reflected polariton waves alter the local electromagnetic field beneath the tip apex, which is then scattered into the far field and detected by a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector. In order to better capture the polariton interference pattern, an additional AFM cutting process43 is typically applied to the CNT array to create a sharp terminal boundary that reflects polariton waves with a well-defined phase (see Methods for more details).

Coupling between CNT plasmons and hBN phonon polaritons

To effectively visualize the polaritons within the CNT arrays, it is experimentally necessary to reduce the intensity of the hBN phonon polaritons to match that of the CNT plasmons. Therefore, we selected a relatively thin hBN flake, measuring 55 nm in thickness, to demonstrate the polaritonic coupling. Figure 2c shows the near-field optical image of the CNT-array/hBN heterostructure at excitation frequency of 952 cm-1, while Fig. 2b presents the corresponding topography image. Notably, the polaritons exhibits a hyperbolic wavefront, a result of the intrinsic hyperbolic plasmons in the CNT array. The polariton oscillation profiles along the x-axis (the tubes’ axial direction) at various frequencies are plotted in Fig. 2d, revealing a clear change in the oscillation period. It should be noted that in our reflection imaging scheme, the polariton oscillation period corresponds to half the polariton wavelength. As the frequency decreases, the polariton wavelength generally increases, but exhibits two abrupt decreases at specific frequencies, dividing the behavior into three distinct regimes. This unusual behavior presumably results from the coupling between CNT array plasmons and the hBN phonon polaritons.

The near-field infrared response of the CNT-array/hBN system is vividly illustrated by the calculated false color map of the imaginary part of the reflectivity (Fig. 2e), highlighting the frequency (𝜔)-momentum (𝑘x) dispersion relation of the eigen polariton modes. In contrast to isotropic materials, the hyperbolic hBN supports multiple distinct branches of phonon polaritons between its 𝜔TO and 𝜔LO frequency range, corresponding to quantized waveguide modes oscillating between the top and bottom surfaces of the hBN slab, as detailed in Supplementary Note 3. As a result, the coupled modes of hybrid polaritons exhibit multiple branches within the frequency range. The CNT array plasmons induce significant modifications to the coupled modes, causing the hybrid modes to display a clear blue shift relative to the original phonon polariton frequencies (see the hBN phonon polariton dispersion relations in Supplementary Fig. 2). The experimental results, represented by blue dots extracted from the polariton oscillation profiles, are distributed across three distinct bands and show excellent agreement with the theoretical calculations. The second experimental band fits with mode with the second-lowest momentum within the Reststrahlen band. The discrepancy between the experimental data and the calculated dispersion in the Reststrahlen band arises because our measurement captures a superposition of the fundamental and second-order modes of the hybrid polariton. Besides, the oscillation profiles of this second band (the three middle curves in Fig. 2d) seem to originate from multiple momentum components, corresponding to several sub-branches within the Reststrahlen band. These multiple sub-branches arise from various hBN phonon-polariton modes4, 44. Moreover, we calculated the hybrid polariton dispersion using the finite element method and obtained consistent results (Supplementary Note 4). All these findings closely correspond with the dispersion characteristics of graphene/hBN plasmon-phonon polaritons reported in previous studies45, demonstrating subtle but noticeable differences.

Coupling induced topological transition in polariton

We then carried out an in-depth investigation into this coupled polariton mode, which led to the observation of an intriguing topological wavefront transition. The detailed, step-by-step process of this transition is thoroughly illustrated in Fig. 3a. Remarkably, as the frequency decreases and enters the Reststrahlen band, coupling with hBN polaritons causes the wavefront of polaritons to undergo a clear transition from convergent to divergent propagation. Consequently, the interference pattern changes distinctly from a hyperbolic to a rectangular (or parallel) geometry, signaling a topological transition. Figures 3c and 3d show the isofrequency contours of the hybrid polaritons at 1639 cm-1 and 1575 cm-1, corresponding to the hyperbolic and elliptical curves, respectively. The green and blue arrows indicate the wavevectors and Poynting vectors. Importantly, because the hyperbolic plasmon isofrequency curve is open, energy flow tends to converge, whereas in the elliptical case it diverges. Our experimental results suggest a characteristic transition of polaritonic wavefront from hyperbolic to elliptical, which reverts back to hyperbolic upon exiting the Reststrahlen band. Numerical simulations supporting these findings are presented in Figure 3b and show excellent agreement with the experiments. Additionally, Supplementary Figure 6 illustrates the progression of the calculated isofrequency contours for the hybrid polaritons at various frequencies, demonstrating the complete transition of the polariton topology from elliptical to hyperbolic.

To further confirm this topological transition, we fabricated a hole in the CNT arrays using AFM etching to serve as a point reflector for polaritons. The tip-launched polaritons reflect off this hole and produce interference patterns, yielding standard near-field images of hyperbolic and elliptical polaritons, as depicted in Supplementary Figure 4. The top image shows the hyperbolic plasmon wavefront at an excitation frequency of 943 cm-1, while the bottom image shows the elliptical wavefront coupled with hBN phonon polaritons at 1563 cm-1. It is important to note that hyperbolic plasmons in CNT arrays originate from their ability to propagate in the x-axis (the axial direction) but not the y-axis. Thanks to the well-defined phonon polaritons along the tube’s radial direction, when the in-plane permittivity of hBN turns negative, hybrid polariton propagation is enabled even in the previously restricted direction, resulting in an elliptical wavefront.

To clarify this transition further, we performed numerical simulations of polaritons on CNT arrays of varying widths. Since our CNT arrays are limited in size along the tube radial direction, we demonstrate the polariton patterns in arrays with different numbers of CNTs, as depicted in Supplementary Figure 5. Polaritons were excited at the array boundary (marked by a dashing line) by an incident plane electromagnetic wave polarized along the nanotubes. When the array is sufficiently wide, the polariton wavefronts becomes obviously hyperbolic and elliptical, at excitation frequencies of 952 cm-1 and 1575 cm-1, respectively. With a reduction in the array width, the polariton pattern gradually changes and aligns more closely with our experimental images, which further confirms the polariton wavefronts in Fig. 3a are hyperbolic at 952 cm-1 and 1639 cm-1, while elliptical at 1575 cm-1.

Observation of a tunable whispering-gallery polaritons

Next, we demonstrate a tunable whispering-gallery mode within the CNT-array/hBN heterostructure. Due to the absence of electronic Ohmic loss44, 46, 47, hBN phonon polaritons are characterized by exceptionally long lifetimes and high-quality factors, thereby enhancing the propagation length of the hybrid polaritons in the CNT arrays. On the other hand, according to the calculated dispersion results (Fig. 2e), multiple distinct branches of hybrid polaritons exists in the CNT-array/hBN heterostructure, which leads to the polariton wavelength changes significantly with the excitation frequency. This in turn facilitates the design of polaritonic resonators. To test this idea, we fabricated closed-loop CNT arrays on hBN substrate. This distinct structure was created by repeatedly winding a nanotube in a spiral pattern resembling a mosquito coil, ultimately forming a circular, donut-like architecture, as illustrated in Fig. 4b and Supplementary Figure 8. We then performed infrared nano-imaging on these closed-loop structures and successfully observed polaritonic whispering-gallery modes (Fig. 4a). The AFM topography of the CNT array is shown in Fig. 4b, while Fig. 4c and Supplementary Figure 7 are near-field optical images with varying excitation frequencies. Remarkably, near the frequency 𝜔LO, the polariton interference pattern in the CNT array changed sharply with frequency.

At a frequency of 1563 cm-1, the inner ring exhibited almost no near-field optical response (dark), whereas the outer ring displayed strong response (bright). This phenomenon is presumably caused by destructive interference in the inner ring and constructive interference in the outer ring, as the closed-loop array can be divided into several sub-rings with different perimeters. Based on the polariton dispersion relations, we estimated that the perimeter of the outer tubes is approximately the wavelength of the polaritons, while that of the inner tubes is roughly half the wavelength. Notably, as frequency increasing, the constructive interference ring first contracted and then expanded. To clearly illustrate this behavior, we extracted and plotted the polariton line profiles along the dashed line marked in Fig. 4b. These profiles reveal that the constructive polariton interference peaks vary significantly with the excitation frequency, as shown in Fig. 4d. By aligning one of these peaks, we provided a more intuitive comparison of the peak-to-peak distance and intensity variations between the two peaks. Firstly, the distances between the two peaks exhibited clear oscillations with frequency, demonstrating the resonance of polariton waves in nanotube rings of varying diameters. Secondly, as the two interference peaks move closer together, the interference pattern becomes more strongly constructive (as shown in Fig. 4e). This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that smaller peak spacing corresponds to shorter propagation lengths, which are typically associated with lower energy losses, leading to the more strongly constructive interference. Another CNT ring exhibiting similar polaritonic resonant behavior can be found in Supplementary Note 9, and further evidence for whispering-gallery modes is provided in Supplementary Note 11.

The realization of these remarkable features stems from the unique physical properties of the materials and the precisely controlled geometric design of the nano-ring structures. Specifically, within the closed-loop arrays of natural CNT crystals, the synergy of the low-loss characteristics of the Luttinger liquid electronic state, uniform chirality, and near-atomic-level smooth, low-loss ring-shaped interfaces enables efficient optical field confinement and the formation of strong optical resonances (see more details in Supplementary Note 10). These properties create ideal conditions for the generation and high-fidelity propagation of whispering-gallery modes. This on-chip natural whispering-gallery nanocavity structure features a diameter reduced to approximately one hundred nanometers. Compared to traditional low-dimensional polaritonic whispering-gallery nanocavities48, its characteristic dimensions have improved by nearly an order of magnitude. Its mode volume is as small as on the order of 10-6. The high compression ratio and quality factor not only preserve optical state coherence, but also provides robust support for exploring strong light–matter interactions. Furthermore, by adjusting geometric parameters or applying external fields, the resonant frequency and mode distribution of the whispering-gallery nanocavity can be precisely tuned, providing a promising pathway for achieving integrated optoelectronic systems. Consequently, single-chirality CNT-based whispering-gallery nanocavities advance our understanding of light–matter interactions and showcase the unique benefits of Luttinger liquid plasmons in low-loss optics, offering vital theoretical and experimental support for high-performance integrated optoelectronics.

---

## Methods

Growth of CNT arrays

The hBN flakes were initially mechanically exfoliated onto SiO2/Si substrates. To ensure surface cleanliness, the samples were subsequently exposed to hydrogen plasma at 300 ℃, effectively removing all organic residues. Following this pretreatment, a precisely controlled 0.05 nm-thick iron (Fe) film was deposited onto the hBN-coated SiO2/Si surfaces using thermal evaporation, which served as catalytic nanoparticles for subsequent CNT arrays growth. The prepared substrates were then transferred into a quartz tube furnace (Anhui BEQ Equipment Technology) and subjected to a controlled heating process under a mixed atmosphere of hydrogen and argon at atmospheric pressure, gradually elevating the temperature to the optimal growth temperature of ~850 ℃ 41, 42. Upon reaching this temperature, the argon gas flow was replaced with methane to initiate the CNT arrays growth process. After a standard growth period of 30 minutes, the system was systematically cooled down to room temperature while maintaining a protective atmosphere of hydrogen and argon.

AFM cutting of CNT arrays

The cutting of CNT arrays for designed structures is performed in the atmosphere using a standard atomic force microscope (AFM). First, AFM is used to locate the CNT arrays grown on hBN/SiO2/Si substrate. Then, a 50 kHz AC voltage with an amplitude of 10V is applied between the conductive AFM tip and the Si layer of the substrate. The tip scans very slowly across the CNT array in tapping mode with a lift-down distance of 90~120 nm. Local anodic oxidation only occurs for CNTs underneath the tip with the assistance of a water bridge. Therefore, the array along the tip’s path is etched to be a smooth artificial boundary. The point hole is etched in the same way.

Infrared nano-imaging

For near-field infrared nano-imaging, we employed a custom-built scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (s-SNOM) that integrates a tapping-mode atomic force microscope (AFM, Bruker Innova) with a CO2 laser and a Daylight Solution quantum cascade laser (QCL). The system operates by focusing a mid-infrared wavelength laser (900~1650cm-1) beam onto the apex of a conductive AFM probe, generating a highly localized enhanced optical field. This near-field interacts with the sample, and the resulting scattered light, which encodes local optical information, is collected in the far field using a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector (KLD-0.1-J1, Kolmar). To suppress background scattering, the collected signal is demodulated using a lock-in amplifier (Zurich Instruments HF2LI). This configuration allows for the simultaneous acquisition of high-resolution near-field optical images alongside topography information during measurements.

Numerical simulations

COMSOL Multiphysics is used to simulate the polariton patterns in CNT-array/hBN heterostructure. CNT array is modeled by a plane with the same size of experimental samples. We estimated the conductivity of CNTs utilizing the method reported by previous literature and selected appropriate value as the complex permittivity49. For the simulations shown in Figs.1c, d, a point electric dipole was placed at the center of CNT arrays to excite polaritons at a varying oscillating frequency. For the simulations shown in Fig. 3b, a beam of light polarized perpendicularly to the vertical boundary was irradiated onto the plane surface to excite polaritons at a varying oscillating frequency. The electric field component perpendicular to the plane (Ez) was recorded over the plane surface.

Dispersion calculations

The calculations of the dispersion shown in Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figure 2 were performed using a generalized 4 × 4 transfer matrix formalism50. In short, by incorporating the permittivity of CNT arrays and hBN, the solution of reflectivity, rp(q,𝜔), can be determined. Polariton mode corresponds to the frequencies at which the imaginary parts of rp(q,𝜔) reach the maximum. For each frequency, the corresponding polariton wavevector can be extracted.

I feel their work is particularly interesting as it explores polaritons of a relatively new material structure (CNT arrays), which here are hybridized with hBN phonon polaritons.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents an approach to modulate the dispersion of hyperbolic Luttinger-liquid plasmon polaritons (HLLPPs) in carbon nanotube (CNT) arrays through coupling with phonon polaritons (PhPs) in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). The authors demonstrate a frequency-controlled topological transition from hyperbolic to elliptic polariton wavefronts and report the observation of a whispering-gallery confined plasmonic mode in the coupled CNT/h-BN heterostructure. The study addresses a topic of clear relevance to the fields of nanophotonics and polaritonics, potentially contributing to the development of tunable hybrid polaritonic systems. However, in my opinion, this manuscript in its current form requires major revisions to become acceptable for publication in Nature Communications.
First, the novelty and physical interpretation need to be clarified, several claims must be quantitatively supported, and the results should be better addressed considering previous works. In addition, several figures and methodological descriptions require improved clarity. Addressing these issues would significantly enhance the scientific quality and overall impact of the manuscript. Please, find detailed comments below.
1. The authors should carefully revise the manuscript to ensure consistent and precise use of polaritonic terminology. Terms such as “plasmon polaritons”, “hybrid polaritons”, and “phonon polaritons” appear to be used interchangeably, which can lead to conceptual ambiguity. Each polariton type should be clearly defined and used consistently according to its physical origin and distinctive characteristics.
2. In Supplementary Information Note 4, the authors state: “The dispersion relations are similar to Fig. 3e, indicating reliable and accurate results.” This appears instead to refer to Figure 2e. The authors should verify the accuracy of all internal references (figures, tables, and text sections) throughout the manuscript.
3. In the Introduction, the authors compare plasmon polaritons in CNTs with phonon polaritons in materials such as h-BN and α-MoO3. They mention that plasmon polaritons exhibit superior properties, including low loss and broad spectral range. This claim should be quantitatively supported with comparative metrics such as propagation length, lifetime, and confinement, or otherwise tempered. Moreover, phonon polariton systems, though spectrally limited to the Reststrahlen bands, are typically characterized by longer lifetimes and reduced losses compared to plasmonic systems due to their distinct scattering mechanisms. I would recommend the authors to reference prior reports on controlled polariton propagation in phonon-polariton systems (Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5301–5308; Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5323–5329; Nat Commun 2024, 15, 9042).
4. The authors report a topological transition of hybrid polaritons from hyperbolic to elliptic wavefronts. Such transitions have been extensively investigated in recent literature, as they can lead to the emergence of the so-called canalized propagation regime. It would be expected that this system also exhibits polariton canalization at the precise topological transition frequency (Optica 2025, 12, 343-349; Nano Lett. 2025, 25, 6, 2203–2209). The authors should discuss whether such canalized regime is expected in the topological transition observed in the CNT array/h-BN system. Also, the qualitative explanation of the hyperbolic-to-elliptic transition based on the sign change of hBN’s in-plane permittivity is reasonable and consistent with established polaritonic behavior. However, the authors show only two discrete frequency cases. A continuous evolution of isofrequency contours across the transition region would more convincingly demonstrate the claimed topological change.
5. The authors describe the observed phenomena as resulting from “strong coupling” between CNT plasmons and h-BN phonon polaritons yet no quantitative coupling parameters (e.g., mode splitting, coupling rate, or linewidth analysis) are provided. This statement should be substantiated with a detailed discussion of the mode splitting visible in the dispersion (Fig. 2e). For completeness, I recommend including the individual dispersions of the CNT array and of h-BN (plots shown in the Supplementary Information), alongside their coupled dispersion, to help the reader clearly visualize the hybridization effect.
6. In Figure 1b, the notation “x4” is unclear. Please define this multiplier explicitly. The authors should also indicate on this panel the excitation frequencies corresponding to the simulated distributions shown in panels c and d.
7. In Figure 1, all panels should include scale bars. If the same scale applies to multiple panels, this should be clearly stated in the caption. Panels c and d should include a shared colorbar indicating the plotted quantity (Re(Ez)), and panels e and f should include a grayscale colorbar for the corresponding magnitude. Please, see, for example, (Nanophotonics 2024, 13, 4761–4770). The use of the term “measured” in the caption is misleading, as Figure 1 presents simulated data. Please replace it with a term such as “calculated” or “simulated”.
8. In Figure 2e, the authors should explain the discrepancy observed near 1400 cm-1 in the experimental data points (high-order mode). Additionally, it would strengthen the analysis to include error bars in the experimental estimations (blue dots) and overlay the analytical dispersion (for example, with a dashed line) on the colorplot derived from the transfer-matrix model for comparison.
9. In the experimental measurement panels (Figure 2c, Figure 3a, Figure 4c, Supplementary Figures 4a,b, and Supplementary Figure 6a), the authors should add a colorbar and clearly specify which experimentally extracted quantity is plotted in each case (amplitude, phase). Was the signal demodulated at higher harmonics? If so, up to which harmonic order?
10. In Figure 3a,b, the authors present an experimental-simulation comparison. First, as previously noted, the authors should indicate which experimentally obtained magnitude is plotted in Figure 3a. Second, please, ensure that the aspect ratios of the experimental and simulated subpanels are identical for a fair visual comparison. Third, I assume that in Figure 3b the authors plot the simulated Re(Ez) … if so, this should be explicitly stated. The authors should note that the only physically meaningful magnitude comparable to Re(Ez) is the real part of the near-field signal, Re(σ_n). If the experiment cannot independently and simultaneously extract s_n and ϕ_n, the only valid comparison with simulations would be between |Ez| and s_n. Finally, this experiment-simulation correspondence could be made clearer by comparing field profiles. Since the dispersion is already shown in Figure 2e, the authors could overlay the experimental data points on the isofrequency contour (IFC) plots in Figure 3c,d as another direct comparison.
11. The authors state: “In this study, we focus exclusively on the analysis of polaritons at frequencies around the type-II band.” To strengthen this discussion, they should include numerical simulations showing the spatial distributions of Re(Ez) across three distinct regions: i) the frequency range where CNT plasmons does not intersect with h-BN phonon polaritons; ii) the frequency range where CNT plasmons intersect with h-BN type I RB phonon polaritons; and iii) the frequency range where CNT plasmons intersect with h-BN type II RB phonon polaritons. What do the authors expect to observe in s-SNOM nano-imaging for type I RB frequencies in this system?
12. Are the authors able to grow or transfer the CNT array onto different substrates (e.g. BaF2 or SiO2) and perform nano-imaging measurements there? I believe it would be highly beneficial for the manuscript to show a direct experimental and numerical comparison between the coupled system (CNT arrays/h-BN) and its individual constituents (CNT array on one side, h-BN on the other) including dispersion plots, Re(Ez) simulations, and s-SNOM measurements.
13. Regarding the sample fabrication process, the authors could clarify whether CNT arrays could be integrated with other 2D van der Waals materials such as graphene, α-MoO3 or α-V2O5.
14. The coupling strength and dispersion modification in plasmon–phonon systems are known to depend sensitively on the hBN thickness. The authors mention using a 55 nm-thick flake “to reduce phonon intensity,” but no data or criteria are shown to justify this choice or demonstrate systematic thickness dependence. I believe that presenting simulations or experiments across several hBN thicknesses would greatly strengthen the coupling interpretation.
15. As pointed out in previous comments, the comparison between experiment and simulation throughout the work is mostly qualitative (“good agreement”). The authors should provide quantitative comparisons to substantiate the agreement. Also, regarding the experimental results, several statements refer to “low loss” “long lifetime”, and “high-quality factor” without quantitative support. Extracted propagation lengths or damping constants from s-SNOM data would be welcome and allow comparison with other polaritonic materials.
16. The interpretation of the observed near-field patterns in Figure 4 as whispering-gallery modes remains highly speculative. The near-field images presented in Figure 4 and the Supplementary Information are consistent with frequency-dependent interference effects, but they do not constitute conclusive evidence of resonant mode confinement. To substantiate the claim of whispering-gallery plasmonic modes, the authors should (i) perform full-wave electromagnetic simulations of the circular CNT-array/hBN structure to visualize the modal field distributions and confirm the existence of azimuthally confined resonances; (ii) provide frequency-dependent spectral data from s-SNOM amplitude or phase measurements to identify discrete resonance peaks; and (iii) estimate the corresponding quality factors (Q) to demonstrate true cavity behavior. Additionally, a systematic comparison across rings of different diameters would enable verification of the expected quantized angular momentum dependence (mode number scaling with circumference). Without such quantitative analysis and modeling, the evidence remains insufficient to support the claim of an “on-chip whispering-gallery nanocavity” and the observed oscillations could alternatively arise from simple standing-wave interference in the hybrid polariton field.
17. The Discussion section includes numerous overstatements (“approached physical limits”, “unprecedented capabilities”, “lays a solid foundation”). These claims should be revised or supported by quantitative metrics.

Response to Reviewer #2
This manuscript presents an approach to modulate the dispersion of hyperbolic Luttinger-liquid
plasmon polaritons (HLLPPs) in carbon nanotube (CNT) arrays through coupling with phonon
polaritons (PhPs) in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). The authors demonstrate a frequency-
controlled topological transition from hyperbolic to elliptic polariton wavefronts and report the
observation of a whispering-gallery confined plasmonic mode in the coupled CNT/h-BN
heterostructure. The study addresses a topic of clear relevance to the fields of nanophotonics and
polaritonics, potentially contributing to the development of tunable hybrid polaritonic systems.
However, in my opinion, this manuscript in its current form requires major revisions to become
acceptable for publication in Nature Communications.
First, the novelty and physical interpretation need to be clarified, several claims must be
quantitatively supported, and the results should be better addressed considering previous works.
In addition, several figures and methodological descriptions require improved clarity. Addressing
these issues would significantly enhance the scientific quality and overall impact of the manuscript.
Please, find detailed comments below.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of our work and the valuable suggestions for
enhancing the manuscript. Below, we address each question and comment and question in detail.
1. The authors should carefully revise the manuscript to ensure consistent and precise use of
polaritonic terminology. Terms such as “plasmon polaritons”, “hybrid polaritons”, and “phonon
polaritons” appear to be used interchangeably, which can lead to conceptual ambiguity. Each
polariton type should be clearly defined and used consistently according to its physical origin and
distinctive characteristics.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions regarding the use of polaritonic
terminology.
In response, we have revised some terms throughout the manuscript. In particular, we have revised
the manuscript title from “Configurable plasmon polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN
heterostructures” to “Frequency-dependent topological polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN
heterostructures” for greater clarity.
To clarify terminology within the manuscript: “plasmon polaritons” refers to the polaritons
generated from the interaction between charges in CNT arrays and incident photons, while
“phonon polaritons” denote the interactions between phonons in hBN and photons. The term
“hybrid polaritons” describes the coupled modes resulting from plasmon and phonon polariton
interactions. Specifically, in regions outside the Reststrahlen band 2 of hBN, only plasmon
polaritons propagate in the CNT-array/hBN system. However, within the Reststrahlen band, CNT
arrays plasmon polaritons are classified as hybrid polaritons due to their coupling with phonon
polaritons in hBN.
To eliminate ambiguity, we have made these definitions consistent throughout the revised
manuscript.
2. In Supplementary Information Note 4, the authors state: “The dispersion relations are similar to
Fig. 3e, indicating reliable and accurate results.” This appears instead to refer to Figure 2e. The
authors should verify the accuracy of all internal references (figures, tables, and text sections)
throughout the manuscript.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her careful review, and for pointing out our mistake.
The typo has been corrected, as shown below.
“Here, we calculated the frequency-momentum dispersion relations of hybrid plasmons using the
finite element simulation method (COMSOL), as shown in Supplementary Figure 3. The dispersion
relations are similar to Fig.2e, indicating reliable and accurate results.”
3. In the Introduction, the authors compare plasmon polaritons in CNTs with phonon polaritons in
materials such as h-BN and α-MoO . They mention that plasmon polaritons exhibit superior
3
properties, including low loss and broad spectral range. This claim should be quantitatively
supported with comparative metrics such as propagation length, lifetime, and confinement, or
otherwise tempered. Moreover, phonon polariton systems, though spectrally limited to the
Reststrahlen bands, are typically characterized by longer lifetimes and reduced losses compared to
plasmonic systems due to their distinct scattering mechanisms. I would recommend the authors to
reference prior reports on controlled polariton propagation in phonon-polariton systems (Nano Lett.
2020, 20, 5301–5308; Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5323–5329; Nat Commun 2024, 15, 9042).
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments regarding the comparative analysis of
plasmon polaritons in CNTs and phonon polaritons in materials like h-BN and α-MoO .
3
In our manuscript, we attribute the low loss of CNT plasmons to the suppression of electron
backscattering in their one-dimensional structure, allowing Luttinger-liquid plasmons to achieve
high quality factors of up to 20 (Nat. Photon., 9, 515 [2015]). This quality factor is generally superior
to that of plasmons observed on other low-dimensional surfaces, such as graphene. However, we
acknowledge that CNT plasmons do not possess this advantage when compared to phonon
polaritons.
To enhance clarity and precision, we have revised the introduction with the following statement:
“ Plasmon polaritons, particularly in one-dimensional carbon nanotubes (CNTs), exhibit
exceptional properties, including deep subwavelength confinement and a broad spectral range.”
Furthermore, we have incorporated the references suggested by the reviewer (Nano Lett. 2020,
20, 5301–5308; Nano Lett. 2020, 20, 5323–5329; Nat Commun 2024, 15, 9042) as citations in the
revised manuscript.
4. The authors report a topological transition of hybrid polaritons from hyperbolic to elliptic
wavefronts. Such transitions have been extensively investigated in recent literature, as they can
lead to the emergence of the so-called canalized propagation regime. It would be expected that
this system also exhibits polariton canalization at the precise topological transition frequency
(Optica 2025, 12, 343-349; Nano Lett. 2025, 25, 6, 2203–2209). The authors should discuss whether
such canalized regime is expected in the topological transition observed in the CNT array/h-BN
system. Also, the qualitative explanation of the hyperbolic-to-elliptic transition based on the sign
change of hBN’s in-plane permittivity is reasonable and consistent with established polaritonic
behavior. However, the authors show only two discrete frequency cases. A continuous evolution of
isofrequency contours across the transition region would more convincingly demonstrate the
claimed topological change.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestions regarding the topological
transition of hybrid polaritons.
The small width of our as-grown CNT arrays (only several hundred nanometers) makes it
experimentally challenging to accurately determine the excitation frequency for polariton
canalization. To address this, we have supplemented our experimental findings with analytical
calculations, as shown in Fig. R5. The results, illustrated in the figure below, show that the polariton
iso-frequency contours transition from elliptic to hyperbolic as the excitation frequency increases.
This analysis indicates that a canalization state emerges around the frequency of 1605 cm⁻¹.
Furthermore, we have incorporated the Fig. R5 as part of the revised Supplementary Information
and added the references suggested by the reviewer (Optica 2025, 12, 343-349; Nano Lett. 2025,
25, 6, 2203–2209) as citations in the revised manuscript.

14. The coupling strength and dispersion modification in plasmon–phonon systems are known to
depend sensitively on the hBN thickness. The authors mention using a 55 nm-thick flake “to reduce
phonon intensity,” but no data or criteria are shown to justify this choice or demonstrate systematic
thickness dependence. I believe that presenting simulations or experiments across several hBN
thicknesses would greatly strengthen the coupling interpretation.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions regarding the dependence of
coupling strength and dispersion on hBN thickness.
Indeed, the intensity and wavelength of phonon polaritons in hBN are thickness-dependent, as
reported in previous literature [Science 343, 1125-1129 (2014)]. As indicated in Fig. R11, thicker
hBN leads to larger phonon polariton amplitude and longer polariton wavelength. In Fig. R12 below,
we simulate the coupling between polaritons in hBN flakes of varying thicknesses and CNT array
plasmons at a frequency of 1538 cm⁻¹. When the hBN flake is too thin, the resulting phonon
polaritons exhibit an extremely small amplitude and a very short wavelength. This prevents
effective coupling with plasmons in the CNT array, and the wavefront maintains its hyperbolic
character. A transition to an elliptical wavefront occurs only when the hBN thickness is sufficient.
On the other hand, since hBN serves as a substrate material, its phonon response acts as a
background signal. To prevent this phonon response from overwhelming the CNT array plasmon
signal, we cannot use excessively thick hBN. Besides, as mentioned before, the wavelength of
phonon polaritons in hBN is proportional to its thickness. Due to the size constraints of our CNT
array sample, overly thick hBN flakes produce hybrid polaritons with a wavelength that exceeds
the CNT array dimensions, thereby preventing the visualization of interference fringes. To achieve
coupling visualization between phonon polaritons and plasmons, their wavelengths need to be
comparable.
Taking all factors into consideration, we selected hBN with a thickness of several tens of
nanometers. The 55 nm thickness is not necessarily optimal; rather, it represents a suitable choice
that balances these conditions.

16. The interpretation of the observed near-field patterns in Figure 4 as whispering-gallery modes
remains highly speculative. The near-field images presented in Figure 4 and the Supplementary
Information are consistent with frequency-dependent interference effects, but they do not
constitute conclusive evidence of resonant mode confinement. To substantiate the claim of
whispering-gallery plasmonic modes, the authors should (i) perform full-wave electromagnetic
simulations of the circular CNT-array/hBN structure to visualize the modal field distributions and
confirm the existence of azimuthally confined resonances; (ii) provide frequency-dependent
spectral data from s-SNOM amplitude or phase measurements to identify discrete resonance peaks;
and (iii) estimate the corresponding quality factors (Q) to demonstrate true cavity behavior.
Additionally, a systematic comparison across rings of different diameters would enable verification
of the expected quantized angular momentum dependence (mode number scaling with
circumference). Without such quantitative analysis and modeling, the evidence remains insufficient
to support the claim of an “on-chip whispering-gallery nanocavity” and the observed oscillations
could alternatively arise from simple standing-wave interference in the hybrid polariton field.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s significant suggestions and have addressed each comment
point by point, as outlined below.
(i) We have performed numerical simulations of polariton whispering gallery modes (WGMs) and
incorporated the results into Figure 4 of the revised manuscript, specifically shown as Figure R14.
Notably, the simulation results are in excellent agreement with the experimental observations,
confirming that the signals observed in the experiment indeed originate from WGMs. Regarding
the mode field distribution: the CNT arrays we fabricated exhibit an almost ideal circular geometry,

Response to Reviewer #3
The manuscript reports configurable plasmon–polaritons arising from the coupling between
hyperbolic plasmons and phonon polaritons in CNT array/hBN heterostructures. Infrared (IR) nano-
imaging is performed as a function of excitation laser energy, which reveals multiple branches of
coupled phonon plasmon modes. Topological transition of a hyperbolic isofrequency contour to an
elliptical one is observed using IR nano-imaging and from numerical calculations. Plasmonic
whispering-gallery modes are presented in closed-loop CNT array ring on a hBN substrate. Due to
the lack of novelty and impact of the work, and multiple significant claims with insufficient evidence
and premature data analysis, the reviewer does not recommend the publication of this manuscript
in Nature Communications.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s evaluation of our work and the valuable feedback
provided. Below, we address each question and comment raised by the reviewer one by one.
Comment 1: First and foremost, the main concern of the manuscript is the lack of novelty.
Hyperbolic polaritons have been demonstrated numerous times in other vdW materials, with
canonical examples including phonon polaritons hBN and a-MoO3 as the authors have referenced
as well as in nanopatterned hBN [Science 359, 892 (2018)]. Hyperbolic plasmons have also been
demonstrated in multiple other vdW materials, including in ZrSiSe at infrared frequencies [Sci Adv
8, add6169 (2022)] and in MoOCl2 at visible frequencies [Science 387, 786 (2025)]. The properties
claimed by the authors (deep subwavelength confinement, broad spectral range, etc) are generic
to these known (plasmonic) hyperbolic systems. Furthermore, the coupling-induced topological
transition of polaritons has been repeatedly demonstrated in other vdW materials platforms,
including in twisted a-MoO3 [Nature Mater 19, 1307 (2020); Nature 582, 209 (2020)] or in
graphene/a-MoO3 [Nature Nanotech 17, 940 (2022); Nature Commun 13, 3719 (2022)].
Therefore, the reviewer does not find that the work provides a sufficient conceptual advance to
warrant publication in Nature Communications.
Our reply: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thorough and systematic review of work in
this field.
We fully agree that the concept of "hyperbolic polaritons and coupling-induced topological
transitions" has been extensively studied in van der Waals materials. Therefore, the core
innovation of this work does not lie in merely reproducing this phenomenon, but rather in the
construction and validation of a novel platform with fundamentally different properties and unique
advantages for manipulation: by utilizing directly grown, ultra-clean CNT arrays as a natural
hyperbolic polariton substrate, we have achieved broadband, low-loss, and directly imageable in-
plane hyperbolic plasmons, as well as tunable topological transitions through hybridization with
hBN phonon polaritons. The distinctiveness of this platform is demonstrated in the following four
key aspects:
(1) Broadband In-Plane Hyperbolic Plasmons vs. Narrowband Phonon Hyperbolic Polaritons
The hBN, α-MoO₃, and other systems mentioned by the reviewers primarily rely on phonon
polaritons, whose hyperbolic response is constrained by the Reststrahlen band, resulting in
inherently narrow bandwidths. In contrast, our work leverages the effective medium anisotropy of
CNT arrays, where the hyperbolic behavior originates from the Luttinger-liquid plasmon properties
of CNTs. This enables high Q-factors and nearly linear dispersion over an exceptionally broad
spectral range (e.g., 6–11 μm). Our platform fundamentally differs from conventional narrowband
phonon systems in terms of bandwidth, loss levels, and mode controllability.
(2) In-Plane Wavefront Visualization and Manipulation vs. Out-of-Plane Propagation Limitations
Unlike the out-of-plane propagation or vertically quantized modes commonly observed in systems
such as ZrSiSe, our CNT array platform supports in-plane hyperbolic plasmons. This allows for direct
imaging and observation of isofrequency profiles and energy flow directions, overcoming the
geometric constraints of vertical propagation in atomically thin layers. Consequently, it enables
practical, on-demand manipulation of in-plane momentum propagation and wavefront shapes,
offering a new level of control.
(3) Ultra-Clean Direct Growth vs. Nanofabrication or Twisting Engineering
While nanopatterning techniques (e.g., etching) can induce hyperbolicity, they often introduce
edge roughness and defect scattering, which degrade performance. In contrast, our platform
employs directly grown, crystal-scale CNT arrays with atomically smooth surfaces and minimal
impurity scattering. This "ultra-clean" approach eliminates the need for complex nanofabrication
or twisting engineering, thereby directly reducing polariton transmission losses and significantly
enhancing experimental reproducibility.
(4) Universal Coupling Platform vs. Strict Frequency Matching
Regarding coupling-induced topological transitions, our work goes beyond merely replicating
existing concepts (e.g., twisted α-MoO₃) by extending them to a broadband hyperbolic plasmonic
platform. The broadband hyperbolic response of CNT arrays significantly relaxes the frequency-
matching requirements for coupled systems, functioning as a universal "coupling platform" that
allows greater design flexibility for hybridization with various polariton modes (e.g., phonons,
plasmons) without the stringent material and frequency constraints of narrowband systems.
In conclusion, the innovation of this work lies in the establishment of an ultra-clean, low-loss,
broadband, and directly imageable in-plane hyperbolic plasmon platform. This provides a scalable
and practical pathway for polariton manipulation and topological transitions without relying on
complex fabrication techniques. Our work represents a substantial advancement in the
development of polariton-based devices and tunable nanophotonics, far beyond merely
reproducing known phenomena in new materials.
Furthermore, we have incorporated the references suggested by the reviewer (Science 359, 892
(2018); Sci Adv 8, add6169 (2022); Science 387, 786 (2025); Nature Mater 19, 1307 (2020); Nature
582, 209 (2020); Nature Nanotech 17, 940 (2022); Nature Commun 13, 3719 (2022)) as citations in
the revised manuscript.
Comment 2: Another significant concern is that the manuscript repeatedly makes claims that are
not substantiated by sufficient experimental evidence or logical derivation, which compromises the
scientific integrity of the manuscript.
2-i: The claim of “configurability” based on simple frequency dependence is misleading. This is
a basic material property of CNT array/hBN device, but not an externally tunable feature that
“configurability” typically implies. The authors’ method of labelling “configurability” can
be applied to most all vdW polaritonic materials. For example, phonon polaritons in hBN exist only
within the Reststrahlen band. In this case, hBN phonon polaritons would also be “configurable”
as one can switch phonon polaritons on and off simply by tuning frequency.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her insightful comments
To prevent misunderstanding, we have revised all mentions of "configurable polaritons" in the text
to "frequency-dependent topological polaritons," and changed the title to " Frequency-dependent
topological polaritons in carbon nanotube array/hBN heterostructures". The polaritons reported
in this work exhibit distinct topological characteristics (hyperbolic or elliptical) depending on
frequency, which better captures the fundamental nature of this system.
We demonstrated the unique capability of our polaritons to tune their wavefront shape and
wavelength simply by adjusting the excitation frequency across a wide spectral range, an
unprecedented feature that distinguishes our system from other conventional ones. Our approach
offers an ultra-clean, efficient, and versatile solution for on-demand polariton manipulation,
completely eliminating the need for complicated twist-angle engineering in van der Waals
heterostructures or complex micro/nanofabrication of electrodes for electrostatic gating.
Therefore, this inherent advantage of our system enables direct optical control without physical
modifications or additional fabrication steps.
2-ii: The authors claim to be the “first” to demonstrate, “a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode
confined in closed-loop CNT array on hBN.” However, this claim of novelty is overstated. As the
authors' own citations (Ref. 38) confirm, whispering-gallery plasmonic modes have already been
demonstrated in other vdW materials, such as graphene. Therefore, the simple extension of this
work to a CNT array does not seem to be a significant conceptual advance, and the manuscript fails
to convey the importance of this observation in CNT arrays.
Our reply: We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive suggestions.
We refer to being the "first" to demonstrate a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode confined in CNT
arrays. Due to the extremely small diameter of CNTs, typically around 1 nm, it is experimentally
difficult to observe whispering gallery modes within their cross-sections (such as the polariton
whispering gallery modes observed in BN nanotubes [Nat. Nanotechnol. 18, 529–534 (2023)]).
Therefore, forming CNTs into nano-rings is essential to achieve this phenomenon. We are the first
to assemble CNTs into close-loop nano-rings, and have observed a plasmonic whispering gallery
mode with a very high quality-factor (as described in the following Fig. R18) and excellent
coherence.
To prevent any misunderstanding, we have removed the word "first" from the revised manuscript.
2-iii: In addition, the authors’ claim of a whispering-gallery plasmonic mode itself is not convincing.
Plasmonic whispering gallery modes are those that travel around a circumference of the cavity.
Based on the main dataset shown in Fig. 4c, the reviewer does not see any clear signatures of
plasmonic wave travel around the circular, donut shaped structure, forming a whispering-gallery
mode. IR nano-imaging shown in Fig. 4c seems rather a result of tip-launched (or cavity edge
launched) plasmons interacting with the entire cavity structure, forming a cavity-like nano-IR
response, but not necessarily a whispering-gallery mode specific to the chiral motion of polaritons
around the loop. More rigorous analysis needs to be performed to support their claim of
whispering-gallery modes.
Our reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable feedback regarding the interpretation of the
observed phenomena as whispering-gallery plasmonic modes.
The polaritons we observe are excited by an AFM tip and propagate along the axial direction of
carbon nanotubes, completing a full loop before being detected again by the tip. Since our ring-
shaped CNT array is highly centrosymmetric and perfectly circular, when the tip is positioned above
a path at the same radius, the excitation of polaritons is identical, and the detected signals are also
identical. This is manifested as completely identical infrared signals along the same radial path in
the final near-field imaging.
However, paths at different radii display varying brightness—either brighter or darker—
corresponding to the constructive or destructive interference of the polaritons. Notably, this
brightness contrast changes with the excitation frequency, which we attribute to the presence of
the whispering-gallery mode of polaritons.
To further support our claim that these are indeed whispering-gallery modes propagating along
the axial direction of the CNT array—as opposed to radial propagation modes— we have selected
a larger closed-loop CNT array ring for analysis. The results, presented in Fig. R16, illustrate that
the path length for polaritons to complete one loop (i.e., the circumference of the circle) is
significantly longer, far exceeding the propagation distance of the polaritons. As a result, no
constructive or destructive interferences are observed in this configuration.
Figure R16. The evolution of the hybrid polaritons in a larger closed-loop CNT array ring on hBN with the
excitation frequency, displaying nearly no interference. a, AFM topography image of a closed-loop CNT array ring
on hBN. b-h, Infrared nano-imaging of plasmons in the CNT-array/hBN at different frequencies.
2-iv: The authors claim that “the synergy of the low-loss characteristics of the Luttinger liquid
electronic state, uniform chirality, and near-atomic-level smooth, lossless ring-shaped interfaces
enables efficient optical field confinement and the formation of strong optical resonances,” is
highly speculative and lacks quantitative support. The manuscript provides no metrics to define,
measure, and quantify the efficient optical field confinement and strong optical resonances.
Furthermore, the authors do not demonstrate how their data supports the existence of or the
connection to the low-loss Luttinger liquid, uniform chirality, or lossless interfaces. These claims are
concerning because they are presented without any supporting evidence. At the very least, the
authors should provide a quantitative comparison of the polariton quality factors in their straight
and circular structures.
